maureen mcquerry: You know, all of my stories begin with a question that I want to explore, that I want to know more about, and that's why I really write the story. If I already knew the answer, I probably wouldn't write the story. And so in my first book, The Peculiars, I was asking, Do we become who our parents are? How much How much do we determine about our own lives and how much of it is inherited either by observation or by genetics? and each of my books have started with some kind of question I had or idea I wanted to explore that way. And so in terms of the mythology, I ended up putting a glossary at the end, which is more of a teaching kind of thing. So if kids wanted to explore more about Celtic mythology, they could do that. But I didn't start thinking of it as a teacher. I thought of it as I wanted to explore these characters. ⁓ and it actually started with a a visit to England ⁓ and seeing a green man. carving in one of the churches. And you know the Greenman carvings, they're they're common throughout all of the British Isles, but in other places in the world as well. They have vines coming out of their nose and mouth. and vines and leaves for hair and they were a pre Christian symbol of new life and of regenerative regeneration of life in the spring and they're really common and I remember looking at that green man and wondering what it would be like to all of a sudden be turned into a tree and my skin becoming like bark and leaves and vines coming out of my hair and mouth and so So I wrote about that. I just took some notes about those thoughts and it turned into a poem. And the poem was really well accepted and it ended up in several anthologies and was published widely. And I wasn't done with that character yet. I still wanted to explore that character. And so he became the first character in the Celtic mythology duology that I wrote.

Terry Heath: So you often start with a question, does working through the book give you an answer?

maureen mcquerry: it lets me explore the question more. Sometimes it gives me an answer, but sometimes it doesn't. Right now my I have a manuscript that's about to go on sub in in September. And it's ⁓ Ten Minute in the Future story for adults. And the question I had was what happens when climate refugees are not just a headline, but they're the stranger sleeping in your guest room. I taught a young woman in science program for several summers at the national lab. And one of the things that I came away convinced ⁓ of is that we are while we are grappling with climate change, the one thing that no one is prepared for are environmentally displaced people. And that's the the next tsunami that's coming. you know, ⁓ the world is already struggling with immigrants and numbers of immigrants and within their own countries and from other countries and there'll be even more. as climate change happens there are gonna be all kinds of environmentally displaced people. And so that was my question. I wanted to learn more about that and explore more, so I started doing more research and that's how ⁓ the book that's about to go out called Rift ⁓ started.

Terry Heath: You said the questions we ask as children shape the adults we become.

maureen mcquerry: Mm. Yeah, I think I said that about my about the board book series that came out and the importance of helping children ask good questions and big questions about life. So asking questions like what does it mean to be a friend? what is happiness? those kinds of questions are very different than asking questions like, how can I make a lot of money? Or what can I do to ⁓ I can't think of another one off the top of my head right now. But I think one of our jobs as adults is to help kids explore big questions but also know what kinds of big questions to explore, what kinds of questions to ask. What are really meaningful questions? And so that's something that I've thought about a lot in all of my writing for young adults and for middle grade readers. And that probably comes from teaching and the Socratic method and helping children learn by asking questions.

Terry Heath: As a child you you loved mysteries. Were you a question asked as a child?

maureen mcquerry: Yes, I was. In fact, the neighborhood kids called me question box. And I was mortified. It was awful. And they'd say, ⁓ here comes question box again. Yeah. I was also the youngest kid in the neighborhood. And so I was that that horrible little kid that tagged along and asked questions about everything. Yeah.

Terry Heath: Is that why you became a teacher?

maureen mcquerry: I don't know. You know, ⁓ I think when I was considering what I was going to do with my life, I had a much more limited view of what options were available for women than ⁓ women do now. I knew I didn't want to be a nurse, I didn't want to be an administrative assistant or a secretary But teaching sounded pretty interesting. And again, I liked asking questions. So teaching was one of the things I explored. And being a writer, of course, was way too risky. I didn't I was afraid I'd fail and wouldn't be able to support myself and I needed to have a job that was somewhat reliable. ⁓ all of those reasons led me to teaching.

Terry Heath: Was poetry another way to ask questions?

maureen mcquerry: ⁓ yes. Yeah. Poetry I think is always exploring questions. Again, coming from a place of questioning rather than coming from a place of having an answer. You're not trying to teach somebody a lesson when you write a poem. ⁓ you're trying to explore something and poems often have that turn that they take. So halfway through the poem, three-quarters of the way through the poem, there's a turn where there's a connection made that you may not have seen before. And that often leads to a larger question. And I don't think the poem answers that question. The poem opens you up to more questions, to more connections.

Terry Heath: Do your books do the same mechanic?

maureen mcquerry: I hope so. I you know, I hope that my books make readers ask questions, want to explore things more deeply. I don't think my books give answers. I do hope that my books instill hope. that's important to me. It's something I think about as I'm writing. ⁓ that they deny as I think it was Tolkien in his On Fairy Stories, that essay that ⁓ he's famous for the a truth ⁓ that denies what how does he say it denies universal defeat. I think that's what hope is, that it's something that ⁓ denies universal defeat and the pointlessness of life. So I'm hoping that my books while they open readers to questions, they still they instill hope.

Terry Heath: What is something you've learned as an adult that you wouldn't have wanted yourself to know as a child?

maureen mcquerry: Let me think. I probably wouldn't have wanted to know as a child how few answers there really are. Now I'm happy to know that actually. And I realize that as I get older, I know even less than I thought I knew. But as a kid, I don't know that I would have wanted to know that. ⁓ And you know, life is difficult and challenging in ways that we never expect. And as a kid, you can only know s I think you can only bear so much of that, right? It's it's that old question about looking at the future, right? Would you want to know the things that you were going to encounter, especially the really difficult and hard things. Even if those difficult and hard things turn out to ⁓ be beneficial in the end. I wouldn't want to know about all of the heartbreak in the world.

Terry Heath: Do you think your life would have been different without the fear of of writing, of long form writing?

maureen mcquerry: Mm-hmm. I think so. I think I would have started much earlier. I was in my forties, I think, when my first books came out. I w I would have yeah. I would have taken a risk. I would have embra embraced writing earlier in my life. I wouldn't have waited for permission. And I didn't really wait for permission, but I I had to wait till I had the courage to do it. yeah. And it might not have been successful. I I would have had to be okay, you know. Writing is full of rejection, right? Risk and rejection. things that you have to become comfortable with. and I think those things were scary for me, as a young adult. Also the unpredictability, I think about this too. you know, with most jobs there's a certain amount of predictable success. You know that if you put in this many hours or you do the these things, ⁓ you will make it to the next level or you will be somewhat successful. There's very little predictability in the arts, and you don't know. what will be successful and you don't even really know how to measure that success. It's certainly not in terms of financial success usually. so one of the things that you have to become comfortable with is that unpredictability. And that I think that for me as a young person, would have been difficult as well.

Terry Heath: When in this career have you been most afraid of

maureen mcquerry: Most afraid. I am afraid every time a book comes out, I'm terrified. I want to crawl under my bed the day before a book's released. And that's because you have no idea once you've set that book free into the world, it's no longer your book.

Terry Heath: Yeah.

maureen mcquerry: And people are going to respond as they will, and they will read into it what they will. ⁓ And it may be something very different than you intended. And so that's very scary to me. It's not just that I feel like I'm going to be judged, ⁓ and that does happen of course, because you have reviews, right? You have professional reviews, you have reviews from readers. Everybody has something to say about your work. but it's also you worry about people's interpretation of what you've written ⁓ and how that's going to be received. So instead of feeling really excited before a book comes out, I'm usually terrified.

Terry Heath: Is there a fear while you're writing it of these things that you're you don't think ahead of these these things that are how are people going to read into this or react to it?

maureen mcquerry: Not as much, no. don't really worry about that while I'm writing. Now neither of my parents are still alive. In between before and after, I did think about family members a bit ⁓ and how they would respond. But no, most of my fear comes right you know, the ⁓ the month my book's coming out, I'd say.

Terry Heath: If your parents were still alive, how would they react to you being a writer now?

maureen mcquerry: Uh-huh. ⁓ they'd be very excited. They were still alive when ⁓ my nonfiction books came out. And ⁓ yeah, I think they w they would be thrilled. And my dad, who really b was impetus for between before and after and his story of being a flu orphan in New York, ⁓ he always wanted me to tell his story. And of course, as a kid, I never wanted to do that. ⁓ and it was only as I became an adult and I got to and I understood how remarkable his story was and how heartbreaking it was and how it impacted generations of our family, that that I was willing to do that. And I think he would be thrilled that I told the story. Heart as difficult a story as it is, he would still be thrilled. Yeah.

Terry Heath: Was it difficult to write that story?

maureen mcquerry: Yeah, parts of it were. Parts of it were. It was difficult to find out about h things that my family went through in the past to bring up memories from my own childhood. but it was also fascinating. One of the things I got to do is my husband and I went back to New York, ⁓ to Brooklyn, where the story takes place, and I found a tour guide who was probably in his late 80s, early nineties, ⁓ when I met him and he was able to tell me about Brooklyn from several generations before. And we toured the streets and I was able to see where these places that I've heard about from my childhood actually were and all of that was fascinating and really informed ⁓ the story. Yeah.

Terry Heath: What's been the most difficult conversation or situation since you've been a writer?

maureen mcquerry: the most difficult conversation. Can you give me a little more context? Do you mean with readers, with myself, with

Terry Heath: I I guess any of those would would be what I'm asking. ⁓ has there been a a time when you've had to have a difficult conversation because of being a writer?

maureen mcquerry: I can't I think one of the difficult conversations, and not a lot of these come to mind, but when I met my brother, as an adult and we got to know each other, he wanted to know what his dad was like. And that was a very difficult conversation for me because he was a difficult man. having grown up on the streets as a child, he was mercurial, he had an alcohol problem, he was so it was difficult to explain the nuances of this father to a son who had never met him. To be able to talk about the very difficult things of living with this person and what he was like, but also to talk about the wonderful parts of his character and personality. and I was trying to do justice to him and explain all of those things to a brother that I didn't know well and who had always longed to know who his father was. Yeah. And that's not because I was a writer. The conversation wasn't but it but if I hadn't been a writer, I never probably would have met him and been in this position. So

Terry Heath: Did these characteristics of your father work their way into characters in your book, ⁓ between, before and after?

maureen mcquerry: ⁓ yes. Yeah. Yeah. Yes. ⁓ the the father in ⁓ the nineteen nineteen ⁓ period was based quite a bit on my my own father. Yeah.

Terry Heath: Do you do that in your other books? Go ahead.

maureen mcquerry: So I come not in my other no, not in my other books as much. Just in this particular book. Yeah. Yeah. My I come from a long line of dysfunctional Irish males.

Terry Heath: You you switched though, ⁓ you said in this in your story, you switched them to female, the main character?

maureen mcquerry: ⁓ I switched the so I do have a flu orphan character in between before and after. Molly, who is the main character from nineteen nineteen. And of course it was my dad, but in the book it's Molly who is the character, so she become so that's a female character. Mhm.

Terry Heath: Why did you switch it from male to female?

maureen mcquerry: Mm. Partly partly to protect a little of the family history, partly because it was easier for me to write a female character point of view in that time period. And she is very protective of a younger brother. And so I wanted that dynamic as well and because it was a mother-daughter story, I really wanted to focus on the relationship between Molly and then ⁓ her mother that was setting so yeah. It just seemed to work well with the story.

Terry Heath: Has being a writer shaped the way people treat you?

maureen mcquerry: ⁓ interesting question. yeah, I think so. First of all, of course it ⁓ shaped the way my students my students were thrilled because I was still teaching when my first books came out. So that was very exciting for them to have a teacher who was published. and then you have just I was thinking about the other day the dichotomy between as a writer, much of your work is done in isolation. So I could say that being a writer created more isolation, but on the other hand, the other side of that coin is it opened me up to a huge writing community. And so in terms of People reacting to me, I've been very embraced by the writing community. ⁓ first in central and eastern Washington, and now I live in Western Washington. So the community here and the friendships I've made through ⁓ writing has been tremendous. ⁓ and then worldwide I hear from readers in various countries. That's been amazing. ⁓ I've heard from students in different states. and then with if you just think outside the writing and reading community, but just people that I know in general people either think, ⁓ you're a writer, that's that's really odd or they think, ⁓ you're a writer, you must be ⁓ rich and famous, which is not the case. Or or they think that you I guess when I say a little bit odd, ⁓ they just don't see it as the standard career and are not quite sure what to make of it sometimes. Yeah.

Terry Heath: looking at the whole arc of your your development as a writer, and the arc isn't over, obviously, but what has it been about?

maureen mcquerry: Huh. What has it been about? Well, I think the arc is important that you mention that because just like in a book where a a protagonist has a narrative arc, right? And they have to change and all of the struggles and things in their life ⁓ change them. And that's why readers really read. They read to see how a character is going to change. ⁓ I think they read for that that more than they read for a plot or setting or anything else. They want to see how a character overcomes struggles and how the character changes through those. So when you ask me about my arc, that's kind of like my narrative line, my through line. How is that yeah. So you're asking how it's changed me or Yeah.

Terry Heath: Well, what what has what has that arc been? I guess you could say a character has something they want. Is there something that you've wanted that has ⁓ pushed you forward through the plot, perhaps, and ⁓ how that coming against that has changed you?

maureen mcquerry: Mm. I think it's made me more comfortable with uncertainty ⁓ because as I've mentioned before, writing is very ha does not have cer have expected or predictable outcomes. So it it's made me more able to live in the tension ⁓ between what I hope will happen and what does happen. It's given me a lot of joy, I'd have to say. part of that arc is realizing that a lot of the joy is in the process and not in the success. the milestones that we think that are going to change us and change our life. Once I get that agent, once that book gets published, once it gets this review, once it gets this many readers, those milestones, you should celebrate them. They're great. But they don't really change you. They don't change your life in the way that you think they will. what really changes you is doing the work. Asking questions, learning, being involved in the creative process. All of those things have a bigger impact and and will change your life more than the ⁓ fleeting milestones that we're all trying to get to.

Terry Heath: Have you had a dark night of the soul in your arc yet?

maureen mcquerry: ⁓ yeah. Plenty. there are times ⁓ I think one of the dark s if you look at it career-wise, the dark night of ⁓ the soul was when my ⁓ two editors left, the publicist was fired, and then I didn't add what happened right after that. I was with my agent for twelve years and she decided to leave the industry as well.

Terry Heath: Yeah.

maureen mcquerry: So all of a sudden I had no editor, the book had no publicity, and I had no agent. And that was starting from scratch again. I mean that just that just flattened me. And in the middle of that, we had a pandemic. And there were and there were some family difficulties as well at the same time. And we moved. We moved from eastern Washington, where we had been for thirty years, in a community that I was very deeply connected to. ⁓ to western Washington to Bainbridge Island where I knew exactly one person. nobody knew about my writing or writing career here. I wasn't part of the writing community like I had been in ⁓ Eastern Washington and in Central Washington. so all of those things it was like all of the things that prop you up all of a sudden were knocked out from under me. And I was having to make all new friends, right? ⁓ as well. So that was that was rough. It was a really difficult time.

Terry Heath: So you really were the the influenza orphan?

maureen mcquerry: Yeah. Yeah, I was. Yeah.

Terry Heath: How did you rebuild after that?

maureen mcquerry: You know, it's it's very interesting. ⁓ I and I would say I'm still rebuilding after that. I had to start looking for an agent again and just recently got another got a new agent. I kept writing. people were very warm and welcoming. so the one person I knew in the writing community here when I moved to Bainbridge introduced me to others. Also I did some specific things that helped. I started a back porch book club on our I had a covered back porch and if I was gonna get through the pandemic I needed to be able to talk to people about books and so we met outside ⁓ around the little fireplace ⁓ during the pandemic a group of about five women ⁓ we still get together. We can go inside now. I got involved in the community here as much as I could. family of cour we moved closer to our son and his family live in Seattle and so ⁓ that was nice to be close to them. but rebuilding rebuilding also just happens step by step bird by bird. ⁓ and I think so much of it has to do with making community that gets you through those dark times and that dark night of the soul. Yeah.

Terry Heath: What do you want now that you don't have?

maureen mcquerry: Hmm. What do I want that I don't have? Well, on a practical level, I have a ⁓ a new grandbaby, ⁓ who is eight months old now and lives in Illinois and I want her to move here. I want her to be closer. But I suspect that you are asking a larger question and you're asking ⁓ about what I want in the writing, perhaps in writing or just in life in general.

Terry Heath: Or both.

maureen mcquerry: Or both. I want to be able to keep writing. I don't I'm not chasing success ⁓ right now or financial success. but I want to be able to keep writing and that means I want my poems to be published. I want my stories to be published. And so far I I've just done traditional publishing. I think that's where I fall. I don't have the the heart or energy to do independent publishing. So that would be wonderful if I can keep doing that. If I can keep putting if I can keep putting something that I think is full of hope into the world, that to me is really fulfilling. And that's one of the things that that I I want. it would be nice every now and then you hear from a reader who says that something that you have written ⁓ has made a difference in their life. And and I think we all as writers kind of live for those moments. you get a letter, you get an email, ⁓ you hear from someone and something that you have said has resonated in their life. in a way that matters. It's made life a little more bearable, a little easier, or made them think about something in a new way. So I would love to be able to keep doing that. I would love to have that kind of an impact. and I I would love to just be able to stay adventurous and travel. writing has opened up the world to me. with connections with people all over the ⁓ the board books have been translated into six languages now. so I I look forward to connections, more connections with people, readers, writers, ⁓ and just others in my life.

Terry Heath: What does it cost you?

maureen mcquerry: Mm. You know what writing has cost me is that for everything writing has cost me, it's had it's had a dichotomy, it's had two sides of the coin. I mentioned earlier, writing is awfully isolating at times because you are just working with your imaginary friends on your computer. But it's also opened up community to me and it's opened up the world in terms of readers and other connections I've made with writers. ⁓ it's cost me my pride, certainly, right? Because you face so much rejection in writing. but then it's also ⁓ given me a sense of pride when things have when people have responded well to things that I've done. I think about time. I've put in put a lot of time into writing and set other things aside to do that, but at the same time that's fed me. So so it's a cost, but it's a cost that has fed me as well because it's fed my creativity. And if I didn't enjoy that, I wouldn't still be doing it. Even though I complain about the cost, right? ⁓ so almost all of these things are two sided. again it's given and also that the sense of security and predictability that you would have with most jobs. With writing, ⁓ you don't have that, but it's taught me to live not always comfortably but with uncertainty. and that's always still a struggle. Yeah.

Terry Heath: Is there anything that isn't two sided?

maureen mcquerry: Hmm anything that isn't two sided. Probably Time to focus on other pursuits. you know, if you're gonna be good at something, whether you're playing an instrument or you're painting or you're writing, ⁓ you really have to put almost all of your energy into that. It's very hard to be a renaissance person. and so sometimes I think There are other things I would like to pursue and I kind of dabble in them, but I can't really pursue them as much as I would like if I want to ⁓ stay sharp with my writing skills. I just can't. And so that's always a little bit sad to me. Yeah.

Terry Heath: What's the what's the biggest thing on your plate right now?

maureen mcquerry: Well, probably, I've got a couple of things going on. I've got a this new manuscript going on sub in early September. So that's a big deal. I have no idea how, of course there's that certainty thing again, right? You have no idea how it's gonna be received, how editors are gonna receive it. I'm not going to an editor I've worked with before. ⁓ a lot of my editors have left and then the other editors were in the children's market and this is a different book. ⁓ it's in the adult market. ⁓ so that's that's a big thing. I have enough poetry now that has been featured in literary journals that I'm trying to put together a book length collection of that. So I'm in the process of that right now. and that's ⁓ ordering poems in a manuscript is difficult and it's like ordering a ordering a book. You have to think about the arc and the flow and all of that. So putting that together. And then I have another project that I've been working on ⁓ with another writer. So a co-authored project that we are just finishing up and kind of going through final edits on that we haven't really shown to anybody else yet. ⁓ that's in a Totally well, very different than anything I've written before. A little bit more of a speculative thriller genre genre. and I don't know what will happen with that. So writing wise those are the things.

Terry Heath: So when this all comes to an end, what would you like to see written on your tombstone?

maureen mcquerry: ⁓ no. ⁓ my gosh. That's really hard. Mm. I think something like a life well lived. Something like that. I don't think it needs to be anything about writing. I don't think it It's much more important to me that I have lived a life that has has made a difference, that has brought hope, that has has been well lived, I guess. And I yeah, I'd really have to think about that one to come up with a pithy answer for you. I did not expect that question.

Terry Heath: That's okay. Just give me a minute here. I'm I'm trying to r tie together You were the girl who asked questions. You were the teacher who asked questions, both from your students and from yourself. You're a writer who asks questions that you explore in your books.

maureen mcquerry: Uh-huh.

Terry Heath: And I'm trying to find a way to pull all that together. I can edit. I can edit.

maureen mcquerry: ⁓ I'm glad you can edit.

Terry Heath: Is there anything that has driven those questions as a common denominator?

maureen mcquerry: You know, I don't know. ⁓ I think I've always been asking what does it mean to live well? Huh.

Terry Heath: Has your writing helped you answer that question?

maureen mcquerry: I think so. I think it has. I think it's some of the things I said, the kinds of milestones, the things that we measure our lives by. What does it mean to love the world well? And what does it mean to love other people well? Those are questions I'm always trying to answer for myself. And there there isn't one answer of course and the answers change in different parts of our lives. ⁓ but we always they're I guess they're big questions. It's like the blind man and the elephant. We always know parts of that because it's they're such enormous questions and so we're constantly learning. We never come to the end. of learning that, of what it means to to love well, to love both the world and and the people in the world well. I don't know if that helps at all.

Terry Heath: Yeah, I think that's a great answer. Yeah. And I think I think I think we're gonna stop there. We've got enough to work with. You were worried about it an hour and we're at an hour and seventeen now.

maureen mcquerry: Okay.

Every conversation turns on one question: what has your life in words cost you, and what has it given you back? Guests are novelists, poets, songwriters, agents, editors, publishers, and booksellers. html:
I've been institutionalized.

To institute a new literary journal isn't as complicated as it may seem, but I wouldn't say it's easy. With minimal tech savvy, anyone can bring something resembling a journal into existence. The trick is making it worthwhile.

Worthwhile is relative. It is also subjective. Possibly undefinable.

Our world is fraught with problems. I don't need to provide a laundry list; the statement is self-evident. Relative to that, one more literary journal isn't a blip on the radar. At the same time, it's an Earth-changing genesis event. Another place to visit new or familiar voices? Check. Another place for creative work to surface? Check. Another breeding ground for creativity? Check.

It's what the world needs now.

How do we measure "worthwhile": by value or volume? Value conjures the ultimate subjectivity. Volume is easier to measure, but against what standard?

Inkhorn Review is subject to my values, my tastes. I am not the one to judge whether its existence is worthwhile globally, but I can say it is to me. The volume is arbitrary in this case. With no standard for volume, measurement is ineffectual.

If a trick is both relative and subjective, how can we say whether it is successful? I've often faced this question while creating Inkhorn. Selecting pieces, establishing policies and procedures, making a place for all of it to live—these things entail a litany of choices. I would argue that their relativity and subjectivity place their value and volume beyond quantifying.

Which circles back to my original point, which is the reason that creating an institution such as Inkhorn Review seems both an incredibly worthwhile activity and one that leaves me on the verge of needing to be institutionalized.

html:
Alphonse had cornered her outside her apartment and he wasn’t taking no for an answer this time and this time he had a knife.

Margret had an armful of groceries and a can of pepper spray that was submerged somewhere in the recesses of her purse.

So she threw down her bags and ran wild, like an unbroken horse, her heels flying off her feet.

Alphonse was lean and long and gave chase eagerly, the knife close behind, gnashing at the nape of her neck—trailing just beyond the tips of her hair.

Margaret was winded and panicked and she tried to think hard—she tried to remember what her track coach had told her years ago about running.  

How running had nothing to do about escaping or winning or getting somewhere—how running was about running.

So Margaret ran until her breath came back, until her pulse slowed, until she could never forget how to—and she continued to run even after Alphonse gave up chasing miles ago and wondered why he had ever started.

A note from the editor: This is the first proprietor's letter from Inkhorn Review editor Terry Heath. These letters will be sent weekly.

You haven't been subscribed to this list. This first letter is being sent as an invitation to those who have contributed to, supported, or expressed interest in Inkhorn, alongside the journal's premiere today.

If you are a contributor to Inkhorn, you are currently set to receive new-issue notifications only. You can ignore this letter, or visit the site to add the weekly proprietor's letters to your subscription—whichever you prefer.

You can also choose a brief weekly digest of everything new at Inkhorn.

On Tuesdays I record interviews for the podcast. As I've said, I'm no Terry Gross of "Fresh Air," but I'm learning. I try to open the spaces behind the words, reading between the lines. I look to create a snapshot of each guest's life behind the work.

Today I released the first quarterly issue of Inkhorn Review, a literary journal with poetry, short fiction, and creative nonfiction. It is the result of months, even years, of soul searching. Not only on the part of its contributors, but my own as well. I'm very proud of it.

It occurs to me that there is a life behind what has become Inkhorn Review as well. Some may find it interesting, not because it is about a person, but because people everywhere share things in common. It's the same logic driving the podcast, with the lens turned inward.

The path to developing Inkhorn Review parallels my own path. In fact, they are the same. Building any business or institution builds its founder. The process of growing, shedding, refining, and growing again belongs to both.

I don't think these statements are going to make anyone hit this newsletter's subscribe button and hang on my every word. This is merely here because it is true, and it is the reason I intend to document the process.

These emails will be written in the tradition of a proprietor's letter—the proprietor of Inkhorn Review, its podcast, "Life on Words," White Rabbit Book Co. and the litany of incarnations along the way. Behind them all is a story, and I hope to tell it in a meaningful way.

Wish me luck.

to use the word oh in poems
no more than five times in my life. I’ve
squandered one in the first stanza here.
Interjections jiggle a bit as they wait.

Certain substitutes—eh, uh, ah—are
heard among the shuffle-tap rhythms
of my dancing or is that sound my slippers
skipping away? Ah, slippers, you lovely

companions, loyal, oblivious,
drenched in soft colors, stained
with droplets of coffee like blooming
forget-me-nots, I want you to listen

in my final hours. I’ll have the soft
harshness of my breath and a few words
left to whisper. It’s been proved that
breaking hearts make quiet noises

only rodents can hear. Maybe
my final utterance will be noticed
by you and a mouse pausing its gnawing,
then slowly starting again.

html:
Everything is reversible, says a man
who has never counted out 24 weeks
on the left-most 7 knuckles of his hand just to keep track of how
many days lying by omission would work
before everyone with eyes becomes an accomplice
or a runaway car. I’m happy
with my delightful birth-defected deaf cat screaming at me
to wake up and smell the vomit he so kindly deposited
beneath the roses. I’m happy
with my cousin in tears stringing along the phone line. I’m happy
with ‘babygirl’ being flexible as long as it’s warm. I’m happy
with prenups and European passports. I’m happy with all that
is reversible, which yeah sure, is most things, but baby,
nothing ever really gets taken back. We just forget
to be happy with what we have. I do it too, I don’t want to
do it to us. Want to stop seeing
what I do: a hidden shine
on the unrippled lake surface insisting
on itself, whispering in circles that
I saw it in the mirror over my shoulder
back when only my Barbies were getting divorced.
They were always walking out of Roman stone court buildings
with their plastic heads taped on
loose. They were bad bitches, bad daughters, bad wives,
and yet they stepped across the inch-high threshold of their homes
and let me click their briefcases open knowing I was hoping
for ten million dollars or a human embryo
gazing up at me like a stillborn lamb.
I always pictured it half-dead so
I could nurse it back
to my life. Never could believe the universe would give me anything
I could easily share. Always knew I’d have to work for it, knew that
I wouldn’t be the only one bleeding when they cut
the cord away forever
only half symbolically.

html:
It isn’t a bird
perched on top
of the square fence post.

It’s too still
and too dark.

It’s a shadow
or a ghost.

But he doesn’t believe me,
just as he never believes
any fact I tell him
from before he was born

which makes every word bitter.
It’s not a bird, I say, bitterly,
but I don’t hold him back

when he runs straight at the post,
trying to make a shadow fly.

html:
I miss the way the wind blows your hair
on the beach with the tide
coming up and the sand slowly disappearing
into the rocky sea wall next to me—
looking into the muddy brown ocean, listening

to the sea birds and waves lap.
The birds are singing the blues
like they remember you walking

on this same beach with your
sun hat and yellow flip flops
as we walked the boardwalk over the dunes.

At the motel, I stand on the balcony
looking at the dark ocean, trying to breathe
until I hear the baby’s cry
echoing through the door.

Tomorrow morning I'll bring
our son to the beach
for the first time, letting him

feel the salty breeze, hear the birds
and let the cool water lap over his feet—
with his sun hat and yellow flip flops.

When her husband, César, “took a job,” as he said, in another state and slowly stopped calling her on Sundays after Mass, she took it as quiet permission to do all the projects he’d disallowed during their 27 years of marriage. ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":2,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Adíos, skunks","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":", Amalia thought, as she watched the last one wiggle under her fence and trot off into the desert sunset like some lily-livered bandit from an old, black-and-white western.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":-0.19999999999999996,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“Hasta la vista, Stinky,” she muttered, and then shook her head at her own silliness. ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":2,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What was she supposed to do differently? What was the message? ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The crows of her childhood were unsettling and unclear, and these days Amalia wasn’t in any mood for spooky messages; she was a grown woman with no time for all that nonsense.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":-0.19999999999999996,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The crows acted guarded around her, too, always keeping an eye on her if she went outside to fetch the mail, to add to the compost pile, to water the droopy marigolds in their cracked pots on her front steps. ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Then her brain slowed as she watched the crows attack as a mob, beaks flashing, swiftly killing the rat before eating it. Amalia wondered if their satisfied caws were a warning to any other rats in the area. She hoped so; she found that she liked the idea of her compost being under crow protection.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":-0.19999999999999996,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"After a few weeks, Amalia’s initial unease about the crows’ warnings wore off entirely; instead, she looked forward to the sound of their caws approaching as they flew up the street or swooped in from the desert. ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":2,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Had any such wives ever existed, or had they only been characters on TV when she was little? ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Amalia was not sure, but she imagined Loupe coming home from a hard day’s work, briefcase under his wing, to find the meal she saved for him still warming in the oven. ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":2,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Better to put you in an enchilada","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":", she thought, as she ushered the tired hen back to the coop.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":-0.19999999999999996,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"But the crows were different, smarter than she’d suspected, aggressive but also charming and sly. ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Eagle took himself too seriously; it amused both Amalia and Loupe endlessly.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":-0.19999999999999996,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Amalia’s collection of gifts deepened. Amalia befriended the crows by accident. When her husband, César, “took a job,” as he said, in another state and slowly stopped calling her on Sundays after Mass, she took it as quiet permission to do all the projects he’d disallowed during their 27 years of marriage. In her first act of aloneness, she painted the dry shutters of their stumpy, brown house the juicy pink of ripe prickly pears. Sanding the splintery shutters in preparation was just as unpleasant as César had predicted many years ago when she’d first suggested repainting, but when she smoothed the first stroke of hot pink against the soft wood, she felt the movement vibrate down her arm and into her chest, as if a musical string had been plucked within her body. Feeling like a divine instrument, she painted every shutter in careful layers, and then the front door, too. The neighbors called the color “loud.” Amalia called it perfect.

Next, she bought tiny, brittlebush-yellow chicks from the local feed store and put them in the long-empty coop that came with the house. The chicks brought fresh life to her dusty yard, peeping and scratching at the dirt with comical determination, like children playing at being adults. They grew with astonishing quickness, transitioning from puffballs that huddled under the heat lamp to awkward, long-legged birds that pecked at each other when food ran low. Amalia became concerned when several started emitting patchy, long squawks that were clearly a teenage version of rooster crows. Ay, she thought, the neighbors will complain.

Amalia did not mention the success of her bright shutters and her growing chicks to César when he called; she’d never been one to say, “I told you so.” But, she felt emboldened enough to start an open compost pile for her garden trimmings (minimal) and food waste (maximal), much to the satisfaction of the local skunks. The compost pile, which César had adamantly refused to sanction for decades due to a fear of attracting rats and making their sparse, flat yard look “trashy,” also perturbed Amalia’s neighbors.

She could admit that the skunks were not an ideal addition to Ocatillo Street, though she liked the way they pranced across her yard, carrying their dainty tails aloft like parasols. And, while their stench sometimes hung so greasy in the air that she could taste it, their obvious enjoyment of her compost pile felt like a private kudos, a pat on the back that she would never get from César. So, Amalia was almost reluctant to see the skunks abandon her yard when the crows asserted dominance over the wilted cabbage, coffee grounds, slimy cilantro, dried petunias, and the rest of the mixed organic detritus that her new, single life created in a pile in the southeast corner of the yard.

Once the crows discovered the heap, they claimed it expediently and with no mercy, diving fearlessly at the skunks like black harpoons from the sky. The skunks proved cowardly against the noisy birds, loping away rather than standing their ground. Adíos, skunks, Amalia thought, as she watched the last one wiggle under her fence and trot off into the desert sunset like some lily-livered bandit from an old, black-and-white western.

“Hasta la vista, Stinky,” she muttered, and then shook her head at her own silliness. She pictured César’s incredulous face whenever he caught her talking to herself, and she felt instantly self-conscious, her hands squeezing the dishtowel tightly, creating cream-colored lines in the folds of her wide knuckles. Sighing deeply, she carefully relaxed her fingers, slung the dishtowel over her shoulder, and gazed slowly around her living room, verifying that she was alone and free to mutter. Up on the power lines that ran in front of her house, two crows cawed victoriously.

At first, the prevalence of the crows in Amalia’s yard made her a bit uneasy. Her great-aunt always said that the hoot of an owl foretold death and the caw of a crow served as a warning, but as a child, Amalia could never understand what the warnings meant. When she heard the crows cawing in the palo verde tree that bloomed in Títi Marta’s front yard, Amalia knew she had been warned, but had no inkling of why. What was she supposed to do differently? What was the message? The crows of her childhood were unsettling and unclear, and these days Amalia wasn’t in any mood for spooky messages; she was a grown woman with no time for all that nonsense.

The crows acted guarded around her, too, always keeping an eye on her if she went outside to fetch the mail, to add to the compost pile, to water the droopy marigolds in their cracked pots on her front steps. Her presence made the crows scatter nervously, feathers fluttering, cawing loudly to one another in warning. Their fear pleased her; it felt like respect.

Amalia had an excellent view of the compost pile from the window over her kitchen sink, and she often watched the crows while she did the dishes. One crow would scout the pile, fly away to collect its peers, and return to eat together as a group. The scout crow never gorged himself on the tastiest bits of the pile before fetching the others, which seemed so equitable, so thoughtful. The skunks never did that; it was every skunk for himself in the compost heap. The crows were also much pickier than the skunks, which ate everything. The crows liked grapes, but not citrus; tortillas, but not cantaloupe; eggs, but not fibrous kale stems. Their choosiness felt classy, somehow, as if the compost pile was not a heap of garbage, but rather a collection of treats to be sifted through with care.

One still spring day when the air smelled of sticky creosote, and the dust was mostly staying on the ground, Amalia looked out the window and found that the crows had pulled all the avocado peels out of the compost heap and created their own mini-pile five feet away from the central heap. She went outside, gathered the brown peels, and dropped them into the trash bin. If the crows felt these peels were not worthy of the compost pile, so be it.

A few weeks later, when the creosote was blooming yellow and the beavertail cactus were sprouting pink buds, the crows grew especially loud. She looked up from the book she was reading on the porch and saw them attacking a rat that had clearly been headed for the compost heap. Her first thought was, Thank God César is not here to see that rat. Then her brain slowed as she watched the crows attack as a mob, beaks flashing, swiftly killing the rat before eating it. They swallowed chunks of fresh rat flesh with the cool remorselessness of professional assassins, squawking loudly as they ate. Amalia wondered if their satisfied caws were a warning to any other rats in the area. She hoped so; she found that she liked the idea of her compost being under crow protection.

After a few weeks, Amalia’s initial unease about the crows’ warnings wore off entirely; instead, she looked forward to the sound of their caws approaching as they flew up the street or swooped in from the desert. They were certainly more entertaining than anything on TV, and she often watched them from her porch. The crows seemed to converse the whole time they ate, picking through her discards, discussing the best pieces, and flying away while chatting about the meal they’d just had, leaving a straggler or two behind to guard the pile.

One Sunday, the phone didn’t ring after Mass for her usual check-in with César. Amalia felt surprised to discover that she did not miss him, though when he first left, she had sometimes found the house oddly quiet without his MMA on the TV or his baseball games on the radio, which he insisted was the only way to really appreciate baseball.

“You have to truly listen to follow the game when it’s on the radio; it’s better than TV. Real fans are radio people. Don’t you see, Ami?” he’d asked her too many times. But she didn’t see, and honestly, she didn’t care. She didn’t miss the sound of baseball on the radio, and with the crows in her yard now, there was plenty of noise. None of the new noise was radio ads with stupid jingles designed to sell car parts or antacids for old men; Amalia felt she had upgraded her soundscape significantly.

After months of daily visits from the crows, Amalia started to feel distinctly that they were sometimes cawing at her about the items she added to the compost heap. The lookout crow, whom she had privately named Loupe due to the way he studied her from above with a critical eye, watched her adding yard trimmings, or tamale husks, or carrot tops to the heap. Loupe seemed to comment on each item in a variety of low caws and clicks, and then either fly off to collect his crew or—and this was more and more common—just caw loudly as if reporting the daily menu to his fellow crows within earshot.

Loupe often remained on a high perch while his buddies feasted on the pile; perhaps his job was to ensure their safety. Amalia began saving a few special scraps for him, which she placed in the yard after the departure of the big group—she refused to think of them as a murder. Loupe craned his neck and watched her carefully as she put his meal out, waiting for her to go back to the porch before coming down for his private reward.

The habit she developed of saving Loupe his own meal made Amalia feel like a housewife from the olden days, the kind that didn’t work and wore tailored dresses to vacuum their carpeted homes. Had any such wives ever existed, or had they only been characters on TV when she was little? Amalia was not sure, but she imagined Loupe coming home from a hard day’s work, briefcase under his wing, to find the meal she saved for him still warming in the oven. She didn’t have carpet, and her bosom would never fit in a tight TV-dress, but she chuckled to herself, doubly pleased by the image and her ability to make herself laugh. Then a third wave of satisfaction rolled through her when she realized she could laugh as loud as she wanted, and no one would ask her in an irritated tone, “Hey, what’s so funny?” No one was there demanding to be let in on the joke.

On a particularly dusty Thursday during a particularly dry summer, Amalia went to the feed store for more chicken scratch. Her chickens were producing eggs now. She felt like a homesteader from Little House on the Prairie. So capable, so independent. Plus, every egg offered proof that César had been wrong for all those years when he said, “No, no, no!” to filling their coop.

The chickens had very little personality, especially when compared to the crows. The week prior, Amalia had witnessed one of her Rhode Island Reds trying to fight a reflection of itself in an old mirror leaning against the shed she was cleaning out. The fight lasted for hours; she had to shoo the hen away to make it quit its frenzied self-assault. Amalia decided that she felt no guilt about consuming such an idiotic bird. Better to put you in an enchilada, she thought, as she ushered the tired hen back to the coop.

But the crows were different, smarter than she’d suspected, aggressive but also charming and sly. So when she went to buy chicken scratch, she asked the whiskery shopkeeper at the Blooming Desert Hay & Feed Store what to get for crows. With no judgment on his lined face and not a single word, he added a huge bag of peanuts in their shells to her cart.

At first, Amalia had thrown some peanuts onto the compost pile, but it felt wrong, like dirtying up the clean peanuts. So she filled a few old pie tins with peanuts and placed them on the ground several steps away from the compost. The joy amongst the crows was evident from Loupe’s first caw to his peers. It was a demanding caw.

“Come now!” he seemed to call, “Come see!”

They came, they ate, they rejoiced, they fluffed their feathers to maximum fluffiness. They picked up the peanut shells in their shiny beaks, flew up to the power lines, and dropped them so they would crack open on the hot sidewalk, ready for consumption. The yard smelled like warm peanut butter and sounded like a celebration. From her creaky, plastic folding chair on the porch, Amalia watched the crows and felt as if she were hosting the world’s best party. Everyone was having a great time, and she didn’t have to make small talk with anyone.

After the peanuts, Amalia expanded to sunflower seeds and some sort of seed-brick that looked like a horrible granola bar, but which Adalberto, the whiskery feed-store owner, assured her the crows would like. She also bought dried mealworms, crispy chapulines, raisins, and fresh grapes, which were Loupe’s favorites. These treats never went on the compost pile; instead, she placed them in the pie tins that she attached to the top of a rusted café table that she’d dragged to the center of the yard when it became clear that the crows felt safer off the ground. Her café table was the life of the neighborhood.

She named more crows. Stumpy had one mangled foot. Chismosa never stopped squawking, regardless of whether anyone was listening, and regularly flew around with her mouth wide open. Sugar doled out affection left and right. Panzón ate with enthusiasm, evident in his thick torso. Eagle was invariably serious and judgmental, and he spent hours rubbing his beak back and forth on the power lines as though sharpening it.

When the crows began bringing her gifts, she knew they had named her in return. She would’ve given up her air conditioning for the whole summer to know what they called her.

Old-Food-Pile-Human? Ground-Based-Treat-Bringer? Earth-Bound-Crow-Worshipper? She smiled at the thought.

On the Sunday when César finally called and suggested a separation, the crows brought her their first gift: a shiny piece of plastic, a thick strip of tinsel that people put in their apricot trees to keep the birds away. The crows placed it in their empty pie dish on the rusty café table as if to say, “We are smarter than those people and those other birds.” Amalia took it inside and used a magnet to display it on her refrigerator, as she had done when her boys were little, their hot hands shoving papers at her, practically yelling, “Look what I made, Mama! Look, look!”

The crows’ gift was instead given in silence, like a test, to see if she would notice. Her joy about the gift bubbled inside her, and she wondered if she should be more upset about the separation, which she knew really meant divorce. Should she feel abandoned? Sinful? Sad? She felt around inside herself, searching, but she didn’t feel any of that. Looking at the glittering plastic stuck to her refrigerator, she just felt important.

Amalia began talking to the crows. They were talking to her, after all. It was only right to talk back.

“Hey, Loupe!” she would shout up at him as he rested on the telephone line in front of her house. “Loopy Loupe! I got some crunchy grapes for you at the market today!” Out the window, she might affectionately shout, “Chismosa! Your chisme is too loud! I’m trying to watch TV in here!”

By the time Amalia signed her divorce papers, nearly a year after César’s departure, she was convinced that many of the crows knew their names. It felt like progress, the measurable kind. It felt real.

The gifts continued, and she had to build a small altar in the living room on top of her grandmother’s old upright piano to display them. Four soda can tabs. Three screws. One playing card (a 7 of clubs). Several food wrappers with shiny interiors. Two dented keys. Several beads. Five bent Jarritos tops. One small crystal. A quarter, a dime, and a 100-peso coin. Two earrings (not a matching set). One plastic gecko toy. A fake pearl hair clip. The silver cap of a lipstick tube. Each time, the crows put the gift in the empty pie dish. Just one gift at a time; they didn’t want to spoil her.

By autumn, the crows no longer feared Amalia. When she shuffled outside to leave some pea shells on the compost pile, they hopped out of her way, but few bothered flying up into the tree or onto the power lines anymore. She greeted them by name. They cawed and clicked back at her. She fed them the two roosters that had come from her batch of chicks, cleaning and cooking the carcasses first, of course. Only the best for her crows. This solved the cock-a-doodle-doo problem with her neighbors, and the crows seemed delighted since they were voracious omnivores. She imagined they also enjoyed consuming their competition for her avian affection.

With the rooster issue fixed, the neighbors began complaining about the crows. She got an earful about it from both Mr. and Mrs. Hernandez when she was fetching the mail. The crows were too loud, too messy, and “a little creepy,” they said. Amalia told them to park in their junk-filled garage if they didn’t like caca on their cars, and then she laughed and walked back to her porch. César, who always believed in “keeping the peace,” would’ve been appalled. Amalia settled into her plastic chair, cinched the too-short belt on her cotton bathrobe, wiggled her tiny toes, and returned to shucking peas with the crows, Loupe standing vigilantly on the low porch wall beside her like a living gargoyle.

Amalia’s younger son, David, visited in the early winter and marveled at her crows. He watched his squat little mother from inside the house as she fed them, chatting to them nonstop as she unpinned sun-bleached laundry from the clothesline, as she walked across the yard to feed her hens, and as she shuffled to her mailbox on the sidewalk. The crows regarded David with suspicion, mistrust, and an obvious fear that he was going to interrupt their routine. He didn’t. He came and went, telling his mother she was becoming “some kind of bird witch” in her old age.

“Works for me,” she had replied breezily. He’d expected to find her shaken at the loss of her marriage, but instead he discovered that she had grown particular about what was allowed in the refrigerator (no beer!) and where food scraps went (not in the trash!). She’d admonished him when he put banana peels on the compost pile, saying, “No, no, Davey. They hate banana peels. They will pull those peels out of the pile and leave them all over the yard.” Confused, David asked, “Who will?”

“My crows!” Amalia replied with exasperation, gesturing to the front yard with both hands to make her point. David followed her gesture with his gaze and saw no fewer than 15 crows in the yard, on the fence, on the phone lines, and standing atop a rusty café table.

At the airport, David called his big brother, Martin. He didn’t bother with small talk, instead stating immediately, “Marty, man. Mama is getting so weird. She named all the crows, and she buys them treats. Treats, man! Remember when she wouldn’t even buy us Fruit by the Foot?!”

But Martin just laughed his slow laugh and said, “Cálmate, little brother. Relax, she’s probably just lonely without Dad.”

But Amalia was not lonely. Her collection of gifts grew. Adalberto from the feed store ordered special treats for her crows. Kids stopped on the street to watch her feed them, giggling, their dark eyes shining with the young wonder derived from seeing something for the first time. They’d seen crows and ravens and roadrunners their whole lives, but now they saw those birds anew. It was as though Amalia had peeled the birds like black fruit, revealing that they held sparks of magic inside, hidden just beneath their feathers.

When school started in the fall, the children began stopping at her gate nearly every weekday during their walk home, saving snacks from their lunches to share with her crows. The young audience called her Tía Crow, or sometimes Títi Cuervo, and they gasped when Loupe landed on her shoulder, and they laughed when Chismosa performed the Peanuts-Are-Delicious Dance, mouth open, comically kicking up spirals of fine dirt. Amalia and the crows were the best entertainment in the neighborhood. All the kids said so.

In the last bit of that winter, when the sun shone daily but the thin air refused to hold any heat, Sugar and Panzón disappeared with a few younger crows. Amalia worried. Had they grown sick, gotten lost, died in a storm, joined a crow commune? Not being able to ask the survivors pinched at her. She gave the remaining crows extra treats. Nearly all of the crows took peanuts from her hands now, and the old regulars were downright affectionate, but Eagle would never even consider such a thing, and he clearly judged his compatriots harshly for fawning over a human. Amalia could almost hear him thinking: sycophants, sell-outs, suck-ups! You shame the Noble House of Crow! Eagle took himself too seriously; it amused both Amalia and Loupe endlessly.

Amalia’s collection of gifts deepened. A dried, white vertebra. A laminated baseball card with milky, curling edges. A snail shell. Two sparkling black arrowheads. A collection of smooth, polished pebbles that she eventually recognized as part of the gravel from a yard renovation a few streets over. Amalia did not return the polished gravel pieces to the neighbors’ yard. The treasures all went atop the piano, where she laid them out like a mandala. Each new gift meant rearranging all the others, a meditative act, creating an ofrenda for her living self. She thought of it sometimes as the altar to me.

The days were always sunny, and the crows kept her company when she was home, which was most of the time. When she was indoors, Loupe sometimes landed on her windowsill to ask for food, or maybe just to check on her. Amalia had happily retired from her job at the middle school cafeteria three years ago, but in the spring, she began working one day per week at the feed store when Adalberto, in a parched whisper, asked her if she was interested. He was old and wanted a day off. Plus, she got an employee discount, and she liked the sort of folks that visited the feed store. Most were quiet and knew what they wanted, but a few asked her interesting questions that she knew the answers to: When would there be more baby chicks in stock? Can you keep chickens and turkeys in the same coop? How can you get cholla out of goat fur? No one ever asked about crows.

One day after coming home from a quiet shift at the feed store, she found a small ring in the center of the empty pie dish on the rusty café table. It was a gold ring, with a single clear stone, so dusty that she took it inside to wash it with dish soap. It looks like an engagement ring, she thought, an old one, the kind from her parents’ generation, not like these new rings with so many stones. A simple gold band with just one perfect, circular diamond, made to last, made to keep.

She’d never gotten a diamond ring from César; instead, she’d gotten pregnant and married fast, a plain silver band on her finger and a promise of something better someday. But Amalia had insisted they not waste money on another ring. Spend it on the boys, the house, the groceries, the health insurance, the new roof, the baseball uniforms, the plumber, the transmission; she’d insisted. There were always more practical ways to spend any few dollars that they managed to save. The silver band was “good enough,” she’d said. César, never a romantic about anything other than baseball, was pleased to agree with her about the ring.

Amalia slid the clean ring onto her ring finger and was surprised to find it fit just right. Tight enough not to fall off, but not so tight that it made her short finger look like a tiny sausage. She held her hand out and looked at it. The gold shone, making the skin of her hand appear rich and warm. The stone blinked alive in the light, sparkling.

Amalia’s breath had gotten stuck in her lungs, and she pushed it out in an audible “woosh” as she realized with astonishment that she actually had wanted a real ring all these many years. She had wanted to feel intentionally chosen, like a first pick, a top priority, a prize. All her life, she prided herself on being pragmatic, but now, as she scrutinized her bejeweled hand, she came face-to-face (or face-to-hand?) with some ignored piece of herself that wanted to feel cherished, worthy, even a little spoiled.

Amalia coughed, her eyes watered and dripped, and she laughed aloud at herself. Crying over a crow-gifted ring! She hadn’t even cried over the divorce. She hadn’t even cried during confession when she had to tell the Padre about her divorce. But this? This makes her cry?! She laughed even louder at her crazy self.

“Caw.” she heard from the open window, “Caw! Caw!” It was Loupe, bending his neck side to side, regarding her intently with one eye, then the other. She twisted her hand around to show him the ring, wiggling her fingers daintily, like a cartoon princess.

“Thank you,” she said gently, her words carrying through the window screen. “I love it.” Loupe watched her for a few more seconds before jumping off the sill and into the air, where he ascended to his usual perch on the power line. He looked secure and relaxed, a crow “about his business,” as her boys would say. Smiling, she wiped the tears that dripped from her nose and hung on the soft skin of her jaw.

Amalia went to the kitchen to wash her hands and some fresh grapes, noting with pleasure how the ring sparkled in the faucet water, catching the desert sun shining in through the window above the sink, peppering the tile countertop with dashes of white light and tiny rainbows.

tags.description:
32 pieces, 32 writers, one theme: what it costs to be seen, and what it costs not to be.

We are watched and don’t know it. We wait to be recognized and are not. When we are noticed, we learn it carries a cost of its own.

The 32 writers range from first publication to fifty years of it, and each arrived at this question on their own.

We didn’t build the issue around it. The issue told us what it was, and we recognized it.

Welcome to the inaugural edition of Inkhorn Review, September 2026.

html:
-- In memory of Galen Gibson and Nacuñan Saez, victims of a greater insanity, December 14, 1992

It was a night much like this
but for three decades’ slow elapse.
It was a place much like this
resting beneath freshly fallen snow.
The solution is quite simple He
wrote, we need only round them up,
ship them to the desert.
If AIDS doesn't take them
in ten years, we can
finish the job then.

It was a night much like this
His "then" has come but there
is no job left for Him to finish
He offered them up
as a sacrifice to His god
Tonight they have no body
to offer to our tongues, no blood
for our lips.
We have only settled ground
of barren altars
outside Buenos Aires,
in a snow shrouded Gloucester.
We have no icons
through which to channel our prayer
save the flattened lead slugs
the earth rejects.

It was a night much like this
but Galen's blood no longer stains the snow
piled along side the library door,
there are no shards
of windshield, bits of skull
where Nacuñan looked
momentarily into His eyes.
There is no blood tonight
on the stairs to my son's apartment
nor on the dormitory stairs he limped that night
to escape what he could not see
his legs rejecting him.

It was a night much like this one
but the walls are bare
there are no gurneys
pressed against the wall,
gurneys I needed to believe
convinced myself were
starched sheet covered supplies.

tags.name: Autumn 2026
tags.description:
32 pieces, 32 writers, one theme: what it costs to be seen, and what it costs not to be.

We are watched and don’t know it. We wait to be recognized and are not. When we are noticed, we learn it carries a cost of its own.

The 32 writers range from first publication to fifty years of it, and each arrived at this question on their own.

We didn’t build the issue around it. The issue told us what it was, and we recognized it.

Welcome to the inaugural edition of Inkhorn Review, September 2026.

tags.name: Louis Faber
tags.description: Louis Faber's work has appeared numerous anthologies and in The MacGuffin, Cantos, The Poet, Alchemy Spoon, Dreich (Scotland), Prosetrics, Passager, Atlanta Review, Glimpse, Rattle, Pearl, The South Carolina Review among others, and was twice nominated for both a Pushcart and Best of the Net Prize.
