html:
It really was a hidden gem—so hidden, in fact, that Hannah walked past the coffee shop three times before she realized it was there.

Birch was in one of the little picturesque side streets lost between the Rue de Rivoli and Opera, perfectly located for Hannah to visit before her 4:30 ticket time at the Museum of Decorative Arts. It was un coffee shop even in French, which meant that, unlike un café, it had more matcha and bubble tea than actual coffee, except the agonizingly slow Vietnam drip coffee that the barista would explain to you as you nodded knowingly, really clueless.

When Hannah finally spotted birch, whispered in pale script on a pale wood panel above a doorway, she pushed the door open. She walked up the narrow aisle between the stone walls lined with wooden benches, instinctively sucking in her breath, feeling like a bride or a criminal at a courthouse. All the eyes of the people packed along the benches were on her as she brushed against their coat sleeves and stepped over their backpacks. 

This gallery-style seating area had no chairs, not even the rattly bistro ones from a café, and no stools either, not even the ratty carpeted ones from a pub. But then the end of the aisle opened into a wide and bizarrely modern counter area that looked like a UFO, with six baristas in white caps bustling inside a glowing neon circle. 

One paused scooping boba balls to toss Hannah the menu, and Hannah, who’d been expecting a QR code, was surprised to find six laminated pages flapping from a metal ring so large she could have worn it as a bracelet. Coffee, iced coffee, tea, iced tea, milk tea, fruit tea, boba, infusions, add-ons, syrups…She turned the pages around the big ring helplessly until she realized she’d been through the menu twice, then called out an order at random, the top choice on the page she was on. A tattooed barista fiercely whisking matcha nodded, and a girl with big gold hexagonal glasses tapped her card and handed her a heavy buzzer almost the size of a frisbee, with red lights circling around it.

There was a narrow slice of bench on the right side of the shop, and Hannah squeezed herself into it. A young guy in an oversized hoodie made room for her, and she crossed her legs tightly under the skinny tin table in front of the bench. When she set the buzzer down, the table nearly tipped under its weight, so Hannah stared in amazement at the girl to her left who had managed to balance her phone, her laptop, and a large boba tea with tapioca balls like eyeballs on the same sized table, and who was typing calmly within the zen calm of her Lo-Fi Girl headphones. How did she do it?

Hannah was American. That had to be the problem. But she wasn’t that American! She had never craved howling prairies and tumbleweeds, never admired the Grand Canyon or yawning deserts of Utah. She had worn skinny jeans, slept in a single bed, never needed bumper alleys in a bowling alley. She was an East Coast girl, from a town whose only landmark was a historical property called “the Skinny House,” and she had been happy there, and even happier in the cramped coach seat of the sleek jet that had propelled her to an even tinier and tighter-packed continent. 

Now she felt overstuffed and suffocated. Struggling out of her coat, she elbowed both the hoodie boy and the laptop girl, who gave a calm smile and continued typing. Hannah rolled her coat into a ball on her lap, balanced her purse on top of her coat and the buzzer, still red, on top of her purse. Like the toppling tower of teacups from Alice in Wonderland. Two remarkably tall hikers with overstuffed backpacks strolled into the coffee shop and headed to the counter to browse the plasticky menu. A Great Dane leading a girl with a high ponytail came in next, and they joined the couple at the counter to peruse the matcha options. 

She wasn’t comfortable anywhere here! It was time for Hannah to admit it. She had struggled with skinny shop aisles and spiral staircases, elevators like rattling coffins, rented clown cars and studio apartments cramped with dollhouse furniture. How romantic it had once seemed to her when the couple in L’Auberge Espagnole kissed on the narrowest street in Paris with the man’s sneakers tipping off the curb edge. Now she had no desire to bump noses with anyone in that cobblestone alley.

She wanted to breathe. The longer she sat with the buzzer’s red lights circling her tightly crossed knees with her legs going numb, her elbows clamped to her sides, the more she craved it. Oh, how she wanted the prairie, great sweeping wheat fields she had never known, wide and wild enough for a tornado…

The buzzer roared to life, lights flashing green. It slid off her purse and clunked to the floor, and the purse and coat followed it. Her tower was toppled. The buzzer growled angrily against the metal pole of the table, drowning out the quiet conversations around her, and she dropped to the floor with her cheeks hot to grab it. When she looked up, she saw that the laptop girl had bent down to help her, and was holding out her purse.

“Are you okay?” The girl asked in English, tugging her headphones down to her neck.

“Oh—yeah—thanks.” Hannah grabbed the purse and coat and stuffed them on the bench, then promptly bashed her head on the metal table when she tried to stand up. 

Straightening the table, she hurried back to the counter to dispose of the violent buzzer and find out what in the world she had ordered. It was alien purple, topped with a cloud of foam, in a heavy ceramic mug like half a volleyball. She stared at it so long that the barista in the gold glasses frowned.

“Vous avez bien pris le ube, non?”

Ube. Yes. Definitely.

Hannah placed one palm under the flimsy rectangular tray and cupped her palm around the mug, which had no handle, balancing it carefully as she made her way back to her slot. Her hips bumped on both sides this time-- people must have pushed their tin tables out—and she found herself stepping over chunky sneakers as well as those big hiking packs, and the panting Great Dane stretched out at a metal water bowl. She was so relieved to reach her own table safely that she set the heavy mug down too hard and a purple wave sloshed over the side, flooding the tray. Much more gingerly, she picked up her coat and purse and backed herself into her slot on the bench. Then, after rolling the coat and restacking her lap pile again, she managed to take her first tentative sip.

“C’est bon, l’ube, non?” The hoodie boy turned to smile at her.

“Oui, tres bon,” she lied, and faked a smile.

She was OLD. That was an even more depressing realization than being American. Look at these kids! In their chunky white grandpa sneakers and baggy sweater vests, when she at their age had worn low-slung Brazilian jeans to look like Christina Aguliera. Everything they wore now was three sizes too big, including the hoodies and headphones—and when had Parisians started wearing puffy coats? Hannah had been so sure the wool pea coat rolled in her lap would be the right thing for Europe, but now she was surrounded by overstuffed black down jackets, and, what’s more, the people were comfortable in them.

Hannah was less comfortable than ever. The next time she lifted the heavy mug, she was forced to keep her elbows pinned tightly to her sides. Her friendly neighbors on the bench must have scooted closer to make room for all the newcomers streaming through the narrow doorway. Come in! The more, the merrier!

She still couldn’t say if she liked the ube or not, or how it was supposed to taste, or if she should have gotten rice milk instead—if she should say it “wasn’t too sweet,” which seemed to be a compliment these days. Weren’t lattes supposed to be sweet? And weren’t cafes supposed to be comfortable? How else had those Viennese philosophers lounged and smoked and plotted their revolutions? Hannah was not in a position to plan or lounge, not with the stones of the wall digging into her spine and the bench under her so narrow now that she tipped forward, her tailbone just balanced on the sharp edge. 

But others were chatting. The laptop girl was still typing, maybe writing a Gen Z masterpiece about love in an elevator, and someone across the aisle was so relaxed they’d stretched their legs all the way across the aisle, which was otherwise completely occupied by the Great Dane, bookended by the two hiking packs. Hannah couldn’t do it. She was old, she was American—she could admit both now—and she could never belong here. She belonged in a wide leather booth at a midwestern Denny’s. She belonged back in her grandfather’s ancient Plymouth, rattling to the beach with the windows open and rolling in the backseat without a seatbelt. She wanted—needed—to sprawl, and saw so clearly now that she always had: the strain of tiptoes to stretch herself taller, all the snow angels and cartwheels, a whole year in third grade learning the splits, spreading, pulling, reaching—

Her elbow, reaching without her meaning to, knocked the metal table. The flimsy tray slid, the heavy mug tipped the table, and she grabbed with both hands to right it, but too late. The table clattered to the floor, the mug cracked in half, and an ocean of foaming ube flooded the coffee shop. The Great Dane yelped and leaped to her long legs as Hannah flung herself down, her palms in the spreading purple lake. Her coat and purse had tumbled into it, too, but she couldn’t worry about those, not when she had to stop the flood, not when she was scooping too-hot latte into her cupped palms with nowhere to put it. 

Ruined! Her panicked thoughts raced. The coffee shop floor would be ruined, and its reputation, too. This place used to be a hidden gem—she could already see the online reviews—and now it’s just American tourists. MIDDLE-AGED American tourists.

Her tiny square napkin flashed white surrender, soaked, and sank. Her tray was sailing away. The purple foam was surging towards the backpacks, towards the chunky sneakers which were all bright spotless white, and she was helpless to stop it. 

Then she turned and saw help. The laptop girl was kneeling beside her, with Hannah’s wool coat draped over her legs. She had saved it from the spill and was pressing a larger napkin to the stain as tenderly as if it were a wound, soaking the purple away and reassuring her:

“I think it will wash out.”

Hannah turned the other way to see the boy in the hoodie carefully picking the cracked porcelain shards of the mug out of the purple foam. 

“Be careful,” he said in French. “Don’t cut yourself.”

And others were helping – everyone was helping, the young hipsters squatting in the spill, careless of their white sneakers, the hikers pulling rags and towels from their packs to sop up the latte.

“Now she’ll finally have to toss that smelly old tee-shirt,” the hiking guy joked with Hannah in French. “Thank you for that!”

The Great Dane, over the shock of the spill, was now licking happily at the edges of the foam and Hannah, blinking in bewilderment, offered up her cupped hands to be licked, too. 

Even the floating UFO of the counter hovered closer now, glowing right above her, and the benevolent aliens had brought high-tech help. The hexagon glasses girl started hoovering up the spill, while the Great Dane barked in indignation and tried to lick it up first. All the young people were laughing. The laptop girl had her warm shoulder pressed to Hannah’s, so close Hannah could hear the music in her tugged-down headphones, and it was an old song she knew.

“Would you like another drink?” Gold Glasses asked Hannah when she had finished vacuuming. “Maybe a regular latte?”

Hannah nodded. A foaming surge rose inside her—happiness, belonging—and her heart was a heavy, brimming cup. The floor was shining, cleaner than before, and all of them were still squatting around the shining spot like it was a campfire. 

And the stone walls curved to hug them all closer.

32 pieces, 32 writers, one theme: what it costs to be seen, and what it costs not to be.

We are watched and don’t know it. We wait to be recognized and are not. When we are noticed, we learn it carries a cost of its own.

The 32 writers range from first publication to fifty years of it, and each arrived at this question on their own.

We didn’t build the issue around it. The issue told us what it was, and we recognized it.

Welcome to the inaugural edition of Inkhorn Review, September 2026.

html:
They were high
school classmates

graduating
from the same

college. One got
married and

divorced. The other
never married but

lived with his
mother all her life

The divorced
one was forever

cursed by his
ex-wife and

their son, for
what was done

and undone
for his family.

The unmarried
one had his

mother’s full love
and care till her

last breath. With
grey hairs and

in stooped back,
under the fading

afternoon light,
when two silver heads

bent closer together,
the two men

both swore
they would never

leave the other one
alone, as if clinging

to the last branch
in a winter wind

Who, after all,
will live longer,

after so many years
of different trials in life?

html:
“I have a new motto: ‘Act first. Questions be damned!’”

I was standing over Brian’s shoulder. “I have an old motto,” I replied. “A fool and his money are soon parted.”

He took a deep breath, moved the cursor to the “send” button, and clicked.

The instant his credit card cleared, his screen refreshed with thumbnail shots of women, headshots, full body shots, demure, provocative, thoughtful, smiling, laughing, on the couch, at the beach, sprawled on a bench in a park, in pants, in shorts, in dresses and skirts, dark haired, blonde, young, younger, screen after screen of images of women from the Philippines that CupidPinay.com promised were close matches to Brian’s profile and were eager to meet him.

“See!” he said.

Eight months later, Brian’s clutching a bouquet of roses, I’ve cut short a meeting with my lawyer to be his wingman and we’re watching waves of humanity in its several shapes and textures flow through the international arrivals gate at Pearson Airport’s Terminal 3. He’s wearing tan chinos, new, and a white short-sleeved shirt with blue pinstripes. It’s a hot September day, the AC is pumping, I’m wishing I’d brought a jacket and he’s got these half-moons of sweat blossoming under his arms. He’s out two grand for the flight and whatever else he’s sent her to fix her car, or to buy her a new computer, or to repair the damage to her roof from the storm that hit last month. And that’s just what he’s told me.

He’s not made of money. She knows he’s on workers’ comp with a fucked-up back, retraining as a robotics technician, but to her, I guess that’s good enough, because the poor bastard’s in love and she’s opened the tap.

It’s been an hour since the flight landed, and I’m noticing a few short, brownish people bursting through the automatic doors, but that could be the flight from Lima, I tell him. Brian’s bouncing up on his toes every time the doors slide open with that whooshing sound, like air escaping. 

He’s lost weight, a good thing. He’s been taking better care of himself since this started. He’s joined me at the gym and I asked my trainer to put him on a program that wouldn’t hurt his back. He’s straightened out his apartment, too, and he’s taking this robotics thing seriously. Did really well on his last co-op placement. I’m kiting credit cards and he expects he’ll finally have a decent job waiting for him.

But I figure that will only deepen his disappointment when he realizes this is business for her until the well runs dry. I’ve tried to tell him, or at least to prepare him, but how do you do that to a best friend who’s cast himself as the lead in his own fantasy?

“Remember when you and Tracy started, how that’s all you’d talk about?” is his answer, which actually makes my point. Just find a woman you hate and buy her a house. But he’s too smitten to make the connection and I’m putting my lawyer’s kids through college and don’t want to talk about it. 

The doors whoosh open and he’s on his toes again. There’s a shriek from somewhere behind us, off to the side an arm waves, people come together, clinging, cheeks moist, and then that big gap-toothed smile thins. He’s flat on his feet once more and he looks over at me, then checks his phone. The flowers still look fresh. He clutches them to his chest, and I imagine the thorns biting through the cloth, but he seems immune to their sting.

I look up at the board. “Lots of international flights landed at the same time,” I say. “They’ll be swamped at Customs and Immigration,” and then there’s an announcement over the PA about a new arrival, Athens, and the crowd stirs and another throng presses in. I look around me. More flowers. Balloons. I should have brought something. I’ll take them to dinner.

The doors slide open and Brian’s back on his toes. He seems to hang there for a moment, and then his lips part and his eyes widen. My hand finds his back. It pushes him forward and I step with him, warmed by the crowd. Kim is plumper than in the photos Brian’s shown me, a bit older, it seems, but the camera flatters, a little round dumpling of a woman, black hair cut shorter than I recall. She scans the crowd. “Brayan,” she calls, and then there’s an instant of recognition when he breaks through. She smiles, big, broad, disarming and true, and when he thrusts the roses forward, I reach out too. I’m standing at his side as she drops the handle of her suitcase, cries his name once more and rushes toward us.

tags.description:
32 pieces, 32 writers, one theme: what it costs to be seen, and what it costs not to be.

We are watched and don’t know it. We wait to be recognized and are not. When we are noticed, we learn it carries a cost of its own.

The 32 writers range from first publication to fifty years of it, and each arrived at this question on their own.

We didn’t build the issue around it. The issue told us what it was, and we recognized it.

Welcome to the inaugural edition of Inkhorn Review, September 2026.

html:
Slip knot between one year and another. It’s like falling
through water. Today, I watched a vulture circle high

above the river, beak tilted at the sun, winding her way
to the coastline. She moved through clouds stretching

long to the horizon. What will happen tomorrow? 
I thought I’d find answers out west, in mountains

or movement, but I only got good at walking 
through weather. I thought I’d know the creature

in this body by now: her red hair and moods, the ache
stuffed in her chest, her changing mind. She wants it all

vibrant and green. I thought I’d get lucky again. Instead, 
I return to the store for cartons of eggs. I scrape frost

from my car in the morning. I scroll the news online
at night. The dog wants out and I let her. Someday, 

years will loop together and I’ll bundle them around me
in December. Someday, I will fall asleep in a meadow

with wind moving wild and steady. Grass stirring 
in a dust-blue haze. Until then, take my hand. Walk beside

this river with me. Let’s throw rocks through the surface
and wait for the splash. Let’s stop and stare at the sky, 

at her wandering clouds, her black-winged birds moving
as we move: endless and onward, heading to the sea.

html:
If the metro made Pat especially misanthropic, it was primarily because of what she did and didn’t overhear there. On the street people rubbed the odd spark off one another in passing or blathered the occasional bit of nonsense or near-nonsense to one another over alcohol — but sitting and standing on metro trains they were looking at their smartphones, having conversations whose interlocutors would, in a transcript, have been impossible to tell apart, or, at best, looking into space. They weren’t even interested-and-so-interesting enough to steal glances at one another (you could forget about ogling!), or to look out the window when the train was going overground. Indeed, the conversations they had were, in most cases, part and parcel of this ‘not looking’. Old-style small-talk still occurred, of course — but it was rapidly losing ground to a mode of communication which made ‘polite meaningless words’ seem as quaintly desirable as, say, listening to an album all the way through or knowing the names of the six or seven species of bird you came across regularly.

‘Serial me-ing’ she called this increasingly preponderant way of conversing. Although it could be taken to different levels and in various directions, all it essentially consisted of was two or more people saying ‘I’m here’ by turns. A group of university students, for example, would be caught (by Pat) taking turns as follows:

. . .“I got a 5 but I didn’t study.”

“I persuaded the teacher to give me a 10 so as to keep my average up.”

“None of my teachers would do that.”

“I’ve got a resit tomorrow”. . .

Or two 40-somethings, we-ing rather than me-ing by virtue of their respective joint bank accounts, would be tuned in on as they ‘dirtied the airwaves’ with the likes of:

. . .“We’re going on a Baltic cruise.”

“That’s nice. We’re going to Berlin.”

“Oh, we went to Berlin 2 years ago. You’ll love it. But I told you about it, didn’t I? Anyway, next year we’ve decided we’re finally going to Argentina.”

“Lucky you. We’ve always wanted to go there”. . .

So boring were they, these ‘conversations,’ that after about 10 seconds of listening to one of them, she was anaesthetised to the point where not even the compensatory pleasure of feeling superior was available to her.

When Pat was on the metro she a) always stood — even when the carriage was empty — and b) did one of five things: either she listened in (and regretted it); or she looked for — and occasionally found — more or less interesting-seeming people within eyeshot; or she looked out the window (or at her own reflection); or, having called them all a bunch of letzten Menschen, she proceeded to toy with them, looking, for example, at the trainers they were wearing (she always wore boots) and anywhere between gleefully and wearily staging a little three-way quantic snail race, which she kept going (and sometimes even propelled to a finish) by three-handedly counting them forward as now Nike, now Adidas, and now Other; or — as she was doing at that moment, on the morning of the day she would die of a brain haemorrhage — she moved so deeply in thought that if she never missed her station, it must have been by virtue of some sort of ‘waking-just-before-the-alarm-goes-off’ mechanism or, why not, psychism.

The thought or thought-system she was moving in right now — a moment before somebody said her name and made her come to with a start — was that of her money problems and what miracles might get her out of them. If one of the miracles considered was death — and death, moreover, not by suicide but by precisely the kind of major biological blow-out which would, in fact, put an end to her that very same day — then there was nothing prescient, coincidental, or even surprising about this. Pat not only thought about death often but enjoyed doing so, thinking-about-death being, for her, akin (she imagined) to what thinking-about-retirement was for the death-blind letzte Mensch.

But at the moment when somebody said her name (as if from within the body of her thoughts), Pat had moved out of the valley of death and into the far less agreeable, indeed, wholly disagreeable brown-and-beige-Möbius-strip-like series of interiors of having to live (possibly) with her parents. Thus, despite its making her jump, this interruption was as agreeable to Pat as, say, finding ten or, rather, five or, anyway, two euros under the bed would have been.

Pat looked up and to her right — and saw Elly standing there holding one of the floor-to-roof steel bars as if it were a staff of power or something. Good old Elly! She was, needless to say, as gently-smiling, frailly beautiful, and doe-eyed as ever. Only, on this occasion, with that staff of power preternaturalising her frailty and with those letzten Menschen contrasting her spirituality, she evinced something which for Pat was new: a sort of shining elfinness — one that made a supra-Elly of her. 

‘Hello Elly,’ said Pat beaming pleasure at her. ‘What are you doing here? Visiting your sisters?’

‘I’m back living here now,’ she said with that slow liquid contralto of hers. ‘I have been for about six months. What about you? Are you still single-handedly making a Bohemia of Paterna?’

‘Yeah, yeah, yeah,’ said Pat not wanting to talk about it. ‘Or in a word: yeah. But so, anyway, what, you’ve been transferred to a hospital here, have you?’

‘No, I still work in Requena. I spend two hours a day driving there and back. But it was time for Juan and me to finally start cohabiting. We’ve been together for twelve years now.’

‘I’m glad you’re taking things so slowly. At that rate you’ll die at a ripe old age without having got far enough down the line to see the essential horror of human existence.’

‘I’d like to think so,’ said Elly in a way which, despite her smile, seemed to indicate that that was indeed her intention.

‘And you’re still A-&-E-ing it up there, are you? Or have they put you out to pasture at a health centre?’

‘No, I’m not burnt-out yet,’ laughed Elly. ‘In fact, I might even be becoming fireproof.’

‘And how many die on you a week?’ Pat wanted to know with an impetus that easily got her, post-utterance, beyond a couple of disapproving comments and some looking askance which she heard and glimpsed coming from the letzten Menschen.

‘About three on average,’ laughed Elly, God bless her (although, of course, she can afford to laugh at my flippancy, thought Pat — because it isn’t her doing).

‘And how’s your relationship with death going? Are you traumatised and taking something, positively revelling in it, or have you become callous?’

‘The third,’ she limited herself to answering — although, being Elly, she’d laughed again, and was even now continuing to bathe Pat in smiling, doe-eyed good will.

But Pat had picked up more than a couple of comments from ‘the audience’ that time, and, irritated-going-on-pissed-off all of a sudden, she rapidly told Elly, ‘Yeah, you said about becoming fireproof,’ then turned her head and gaze to the left — and immediately encountered the trouble she was after: a pair of 50-something-year-old female eyes looking daggers at her. Pat’s first reaction was to look away — but then, given a shove back into the ring by her own irritation, and having, she hoped, succeeded in turning that initial movement towards flight into what appeared a flurry of blinks, she went on to do what, as she did it, converted her mounting anger into a loud, more-than-a-little maniacal internal laugh: staring straight back at the woman’s daggers, she opened her own eyes as wide (literally) as she could and..... made the woman look away.

The woman, it’s true, let off a Parthian ‘Lunatic’ as she came scrambling down off her redoubt — but Pat simply took that as the compliment it undoubtedly essentially was.

For a moment, she was very much ready for the next one — very much tempted, that was, to look further left and so take on the next ‘fucker.’ But then an absurd vision of it actually coming to blows interceded (since, whatever else happened, she wasn’t going to descend to arguing with them), and seeing herself knocking them around and down with the martial arts skills she in no way possessed, she turned back to Elly with such a broad smile on her face that the corners of Elly’s mirror smile seemed to go up past the tip of her nose.

‘Well,’ said Pat. ‘We’ve only got a couple of stations left. So you’d better hurry up and tell me first about your family and then about the mad dogs and comatose cats which, your family being your family, are almost certainly lying somewhere within its folds.’

As she strode uphill from the station to her brother’s flat, Pat was giving herself what, friendliness of tone notwithstanding, amounted to a talking to.

It’s not as if I’m the Grim Reaper’s next door neighbour, whom he regularly borrows sugar from, she was telling herself as part of a ‘necessary’, self-prescribed coming-back-down-to-earth process after her ‘exploit’ on the metro. Yes, she thought, they’re death-blind, but— 

But what? she demanded suddenly, unable to take ‘this shit’ even from herself. They fucking started it!

And she would undoubtedly have been punished for her ‘heroic victory’ qua hubris with a nice little, tight little anxiety-generating circle of Hell on earth if, just then, a big ginger tom hadn’t appeared. 

He was sauntering down the middle of the street, holding his tail up as though the slight effort that required had been the essence of play and so art. Having become inwardly silent at the sight of him, Pat nodded him a wordless hello. He, for his part, not only regarded her face toward face, but continued to do so. Thus, turning his head as they drew closer and closer to the line beyond which — she on the pavement and he in the middle of the road — they’d walk and saunter into one another’s pasts, he gave her back far more than she’d given him.

Sufficient happiness, she would, perhaps, have called what he gave her if she hadn’t still been mute inside at the moment when she felt it most.

Only, when she and he had, in fact, already crossed said ‘line’, and Pat, picturing the intercom panel to herself, was beginning (with reemergent language) to try to pre-work-out which of the innumerable unmarked buzzers her brother’s was, she suddenly decided to look back over her shoulder — in order to see what the ginger tom was doing now.

What he was doing was two things: sauntering down the middle of the street and looking over his shoulder at Pat.

32 pieces, 32 writers, one theme: what it costs to be seen, and what it costs not to be.

We are watched and don’t know it. We wait to be recognized and are not. When we are noticed, we learn it carries a cost of its own.

The 32 writers range from first publication to fifty years of it, and each arrived at this question on their own.

We didn’t build the issue around it. The issue told us what it was, and we recognized it.

Welcome to the inaugural edition of Inkhorn Review, September 2026.

html:
Sunday morning at the art gallery
soaking up Picasso pen and ink
sketches. In a sunny corner

Sleeping Woman—War, Peace
marked XXII, one hand on wrist,
face resting on her forearm,
eyes closed, hair brushed back.
horizontal lines. Serene. Secure.

Security breach at home. Laptop
says our accounts are at zero.
I squint, put on sunglasses. Tell
Evan to change the TV channel.
Shut off my phone, no, call the
bank, credit card companies.
 Urgency breaks into my ears zinging
a high electronic beep. Cancel cards.
Tense wait for bank to call back. Scotty comes in with muffins, assorted.

The leak cascades downward, upward,
branches out like an oak tree, each
loss unique like a snowflake, rising
into a flood. I sit at the glass table,
watching data sift out, drift up like
sand from sea caves under the house.
Quick, Scotty. Dollar Store. Sandbags.

An email arrives: Don’t do a thing if you
value your life. A tall man stands
at the front door. Now it’s personal.
I can’t lose my identity before next week’s
gallbladder operation. I light a cigarette
to go with a muffin. Credit rating nosedives.

With all data rotting on the bottom of the river, I rest my head on the glass table. Arms folded,
eyes closed, hair brushed back, horizontal lines,
something to hold on to, War and Peace.

html:
asleep with a blanket, her cheek
on her chin as a pillow,
the whippet tucked under
an armpit and tea on the table
you could lift and pour over
a baby – a cigarette a shinbone
of bending and mottling ash.
I leave on a ten minute
wine-run – the diorama
stable. light moves across
the soft foot hills of features:
a sock stretching over an ankle.

html:
“Give me your arm, Dad.”

“I’m fine.  What the frick, I’m not a complete invalid. Not yet.”

Jim stood inside the garage looking up at his father who stood in the laundry room doorway.  Harold was studying the steps that led down into the garage.  The son dropped his extended hand to his side and tensed as the seventy-nine-year-old contemplated the task before him.

“I just got to remember what the physical therapist taught me, ‘The pain is the worst if the cane’s not first.’” The old man slowly bent over and placed his cane onto the first step with his right hand.  Then came the right leg. Then the left. The procedure was slowly repeated until he safely made the garage floor.

Harold, pleased with his effort, tapped his cane smartly on the garage floor and straightened his back.  “You take the small victories when you can get them.”

“Sure, Dad.  You really nailed the landing.  You got two tens and a seven.”

“A seven? The Russian judge?” Harold asked.

Jim nodded, finishing an old joke they had shared more than a few times.

“Turn on some more lights, will ya Jimmy?”

Jim pulled on strings hanging from the ceiling, igniting dusty bulbs that sputtered to life.  The newly retired son looked around at memories, memories hanging from the ceiling, memories leaning against the walls, memories tucked into corners.  He walked over to one of several shelving units and pulled a canvas bag from the top shelf.  After rummaging around a bit, he pulled out an old baseball glove and tried it on.

“Ha! Still fits.”  Grinning, he held it up for his father to see. “It could use a little mink oil.”

“Yeah, so could I.  That leather looks about as stiff and wrinkled as my ass.”

“Ahhh. Thanks for that image, pops.” Jim flexed the glove and gently rapped his fist into the palm of it.  “This baby scooped up a ton of grounders you hit to me.”

A smile on Harold’s face shriveled. “And now, instead of swinging a baseball bat, I’m struggling to handle a cane.”

Jim pondered his response.  His father had never been one much to complain or fish for sympathy. “You’ve come a long way since you fell, Dad.”

Harold offered a small, silent nod.

“So what did you want to show me out here?” asked Jim, his eyes sweeping around a crowded garage.

“Everything, I guess. I’d like to get this thing cleaned out now, while I’m still alive, and not leave this mess to you and your sister Julie after I’m gone.”

“You got plans for leaving soon?”  The smile on Jim’s face couldn’t hide the concern cornered in his eyes.

“No, but before I get too many nails in my coffin, I’d like to tidy up various loose ends like the stuff in here I no longer use.”

“Nails in your coffin?  Jeez, Dad, have you got a suit all picked out for the occasion?”

Harold ran a hand over a smooth scalp that once sported a coarse field of thick brown hair. Ignoring his son, he used his cane to point at a bike hanging from the ceiling.

“There’s one of them nails.  I haven’t ridden that thing in ten, maybe 20 years.  Crap, I can’t even get it down, let alone ride it.” 

Jim looked back and forth between the bike and its former rider.  Keeping a long sigh to himself, he walked over to a corner workbench and picked up a file with a wooden handle, noting how the wood had been worn smooth by his father’s hands, hands that had used the file to fix toys, maintain lawn equipment, and shape the sharp edges of a home.

“And that’s frustrating, too,” Harold said, now gesturing towards the garden tools hanging from a pegboard. “I haven’t touched a hoe in two years.” 

Jim’s eyebrows raised high above his broadening smile.  His father preempted any retort with, “Spare me the joke.”

Harold continued his contemplation. “Damn, I’d give a pretty penny to be able to walk down the hill and plant some vegetables.  I miss working that garden.  I miss picking cucumbers and bringing them to your mother.  She always said there was nothing like freshly picked cukes. Yeah, that’s a big nail in the coffin.”

Harold walked over to inspect the various garden tools.  Jim stared at his father’s back, a back that had lifted large logs, pushed loaded wheelbarrows uphill, and swept him and his sister together and carried them off to bed. He went to his aged parent and put a hand on his shoulder.

“You know what I miss?” Jim said. “I miss the dad who, when he got laid off from his job at the railroad, picked up work on a garbage truck while he went back to school and got trained to be an electrician.  I miss that dad that went up against a wall and didn’t miss a beat in finding a way around it, over it, or through it.”

Harold snorted. “You miss him? I’ve been looking for that sorry ass butthead for years.”

“He’s still there. He just can’t get out from behind a big cloud of pout.”

Harold looked sharply at his son while his hand clenched his cane.  Shrugging off the hand on his shoulder he said, “That what you think I’m doing?  Pouting?”  His head began to bob and his jaw work back and forth. “You think it’s easy learning how to walk again? You think it’s easy getting on without your mother?”  

Harold looked around the garage at the various tools he no longer brandished. Closing his eyes, his head spun with endless doctor appointments, age spots, and a lonely kitchen table. “Maybe you ought to try getting old, Jimmy, before you dispense with all your wisdom. Maybe you ought to have a bulging pill case, a cane, and safety grips all over your shower.” 

Harold’s volume increased. “Maybe you ought to shit your pants a few times in your adult diaper before telling others how they should act.”  

He shuffled within an arm’s length of his son, staring intently.  

Harold continued with clenched teeth. “When’s the last time you felt diminished?  When’s the last time you didn’t feel like a man?”  His quavering voice matched the wobbling cane at his side. Neither man said anything, each reflecting the pain on the other’s face. 

The old man looked away from his son. His breathing slowed. Jim reached out his hand, covering his father’s claw-like fingers that still worked the cane. Harold glanced towards the cane and then stared again into his son’s eyes.  

“Oh, yeah?” he said.  His face softened some while he took his free hand and covered his firstborn’s hand, making a stack of three.  Jim raised an eyebrow— and then his remaining free hand—placing it over the stack of three, giving a soft squeeze to the pile of fingers.

Harold grunted a laugh. “Get me a goddamn chair before I fall down, will ya?”

Jim strode to the lawn chairs neatly hanging against a wall.  He positioned two of them near the steps leading into the house.  When Harold shuffled towards the chairs, Jim reached out to take his father’s elbow but withdrew when Harold shook his head firmly.  The son let his father slowly lower his frame into one of the chairs.  Jim sat quietly next to him.  Both men carefully avoid eye contact, looking instead at their past lives hanging from hooks, languishing on shelves, collecting layers of dust.

Harold cleared his throat. “It . . . damn, it’s hard not being able to do what you once enjoyed, what was once routine, what once was normal.  It’s hard not being  . . . able.”

html:
Born in captivity, Flaco conversed
With visitors through bars, his mighty wings
Becalmed in Central Park’s Zoo, a locked ward’s
Parameter of hunger for freedom.
Small mammals fed to Flaco filled him up,
Since blood demands more blood, while reminding
The thirteen-year-old predator of his
Entrapment, power’s raw futility.
Little disturbed the blue work of dreaming
Till rascals clipped meshed wires – and he flew free,
Uniting citizens who chronicled
His accidental liberation day.
Long cloistered, this Eurasian eagle-owl
Exerted untried muscles, mastering
Pale fire, exploring, cautiously at first,
The Upper West Side’s ecstasy of sky,
Becoming Manhattan’s reigning rat czar,
His art the genius of inspiring awe
While commandeering new celebrity.
Don’t make me tell you how he crashed and slipped,
A lesson in humility unfit
For such a rara avis resplendent.
Did Flaco love us back? We thought he did.

Chase watched with shame as his idol, swaying and heavy-footed, forgot to close the truck’s door while dropping his keys on the ground, staggered to the house with overly deliberate steps. In the kitchen, Daddy-O rummaged the cabinets for his “malaria medicine.” Chase watched with apprehension.  

“Where’s my malaria medicine?” Daddy-O bellowed. More rummaging, then, “Elaine, where’s the malaria medicine?” The words “malaria” and “medicine” came out slurred as “ma-lare” and “med-sin.” 

Chase hurried to the kitchen. “Dad, Mom’s not here. Remember . . . Mom moved to Miami.”  

Reeking of cigar and gin, Daddy-O squinted at Chase, impersonating Blackbeard in a growly voice. “Go find her, Jack.” 

“Captain,” Chase lied, “we don’t know where your medicine is.” 

“No one leaves this ship until we find the med-sin and the scurvy dog who took it.” Just then, something caught Daddy-O’s attention. From the top of the refrigerator, he brought down the empty Beefeater’s bottle, holding it up like “Exhibit A.” Then he looked Chase sternly in the eyes. “And just what might be this, Jack, me boy?” 

“Before she left, Mom said to empty it,” Chase stammered, “so, uh, you wouldn’t drive with a . . . snootful.”

“Snootful! You think the captain can’t hold his own med-sin, eh?” Daddy-O pulled off his belt. “Damn you, Mister Jack, that’s mutiny aboard my ship! It’ll be a cat-o-nine-tails for you, and a night in the rigging.” He slurred each “s.”   

“Dad, it’s me. Chase.” 

“How dare you trifle with the master of this ship!?” He threw the bottle down, shattering it on the floor. Chase stepped back, falling over a chair behind him. The belt caught him across the back and chest, burning like a hot iron.  

“OW!” Chase screamed. “OW! STOP!” He shoved the chair at his father and scurried under the grand piano like a frightened mouse. Daddy-O got the kitchen broom, thrusting it under the piano. Chase crouched, dodging the broom.  

“Take your punishment like a man!”  

“Let's get new malaria medicine. I can drive us, okay?”  

Not listening, his father found plastic plates stacked on the kitchen counter. He threw a plate under the piano like a Frisbee. The plate hit the floor, skipped once, and flew under the piano, hitting the wall next to Chase. The next plate hit Chase on the shin. An electric shock pain shot through Chase’s leg. When he curled into a ball, another plate hit him in the back. His father laughed fiendishly.

“Argh, come out and face your--” Daddy-O stopped. A plate clattered on the floor. Chase peeked out. Daddy-O collapsed, grabbing his chest with both hands.   

Chase scrambled to his side. “What is it!? Is it your heart!?”

Between grimaces, Daddy-O uttered the word “pills.”

Chase ran to the bedroom and grabbed the nitroglycerin pills on the dresser. Flat on his back, Daddy-O’s eyes scanned the room as if seeing it for the last time. 

“Here.” Chase shook out a tiny white pill. “Open your mouth!” Chase placed the pill on his tongue. 

“Lie still while I call the ambulance.” 

“No! Get me to the bedroom.”

“You need a doctor.”

“No hospitals! The pill’s working.” 

Now his father was sober. 

“Can you make it to the bedroom?” 

“I’ll go on my hands and knees.”

Chase sat in the bedroom watching his sleeping father’s chest rise and fall under the sheet. Then the boy stood in front of the mirror. The welts on his back were bright red. 

He went to his bedroom, grabbed his camping gear, and tiptoed out. Dockside, he hopped aboard Zorro, the sailing dinghy Daddy-O and he built. Chase untied the mooring lines and shoved off. He rowed out into open water and raised the mainsail and jib. In the monsoon month of June, an early-morning sail to the island would avoid the afternoon heat that formed the worst squalls.

half of my split molar splintered in my mouth
and I surveyed it like an ape considers a snowglobe
before casually discarding it
                                        but I did not tell my wife

my mind is wrought with thanatopsis
while my body worriedly works
to contain my blood, bones, and organs
                                         but I do not tell my wife

a tight right glute causes low back spasms
while my prostate balloons turgid
and luteinizing hormone too low for kids
                                          but I cannot tell my wife

I woolgather often, the narrator of Dos’s Notes,
what was his name, perchance tomorrow I will be
a roach, I have no spout, and I must steam
                                           but I will not waste her time

maybe in the Himalayas
                    time stands alongside you
                                        rather than race ahead
I would like to ask a mountain man
                    but I do not believe
                                        I will have the chance

perhaps my sweet wife will sojourn in that cold high place when this body ignominiously fails,
          with whatever goo or sludge or salty sediment that remains,           and:

                    although no grace, I feel no pain,
                    it is a pleasure, and you are not
                    obliged to fulfill dreams of dust
                    I hope someone will tell her.

html:
Ava glides over the polished floorboards of her sixth-floor Flatbush apartment to the music of the New York Philharmonic performing a Strauss waltz. Her satin-and-suede dance shoes hardly make a sound. With eyes closed, her hands grasp an imaginary partner that she changes every few days depending on who she sees in real life – always a handsome man that she mentally dresses in 19th-century evening attire.

A loud knock on her door brings her back from her dream of whirling couples in a Viennese ballroom. She squints through the door’s peephole. A stout middle-aged woman, barely tall enough to be seen, stands in the hallway. Ava slides two bolts back, twists the deadbolt, and opens the door on the chain.

“Yes, Mrs. Lanchart?”

“I’m sorry, Ava, but you’re playing that music too loud again. Would you please turn it down?”

“I’m Sorry, Mrs. Lanchart, I keep forgetting where I am.”

“Why do you play that old music, anyway? With the boys back from Vietnam, the bands are playing hot stuff in the clubs. You should come with Harold and me . . . get out of that damn apartment for a change.”

“Thanks for the offer, but I’m too tired after work.”

“You’re not working Saturdays.”

“Thanks again for the offer. I’ll turn the music down.”

Ava smiles through the narrow opening, knowing Mrs. Lanchart means well. Her neighbor just shakes her head and retreats. Ava shudders at the thought of visiting a smoke-filled nightclub where the music’s so loud you can’t hold a conversation, not that she has much to say. She moves to the stereo that has quieted on its own. Turning the LP over, Ava queues the needle and lowers the volume. Everyone has a different tolerance for sound, and Mrs. Lanchart is her most sensitive neighbor so far.

The Blue Danube flows from the stereo’s speakers. Ava continues to waltz – one-two-three, one-two-three – her willowy body barely disturbing the moist winter air. The heat radiators cough, ostensibly in time with the music. After an hour of dancing she returns from Vienna to her walkup apartment in Flatbush, to 1973 and her job as a junior accountant with one of New York City’s largest law firms. She dabs at her glistening face with a towel, sips a glass of Riesling, and remembers back a decade.

“So what are you gonna do after we graduate?” Emily, Ava’s only high-school friend, asked.

“Haven’t you heard? I’ve been accepted at Columbia.”

“How the hell can your parents afford that? Your Pop must be doin’ a whole bunch of engine rebuilds.”

“I received a scholarship and I’ve saved money from working at my uncle’s bodega.”

“Lucky damn you. Meanwhile, I’ll be waitressing for the rest of my life.” 

“Don’t say that, Em. Something will come your way.”

“Yeah, I just hope he’s handsome and rich . . . well, at least rich.”

The girls had laughed.

Emily asked, “So what are you gonna take for sixth period elective?”

“I don’t know. I might take ballroom dancing from Mrs. Flanalle.”

“What for?”

“There may be boys there. I might actually get to . . . you know, touch one.”

Emily giggled. “Oh you’ll touch one all right. I took that class at the end of sophomore year. I had enough boys stomp on my feet to last a lifetime. And all they really wanted to do was crunch my boobs.”

“I won’t have that problem,” Ava said and frowned.

“Hey, hey. It’ll be fun. Enjoy it. It’ll probably be the only time you’ll do ballroom dancing, until you’re gray-haired and they pair you with some old geezer at the rest home.”

“I’m already feeling old.”

“Not hardly.”

Ava reported to the gymnasium for the first dance class. Fourteen other kids had also signed up. With eleven girls and four boys, Ava did most of her dancing with girls, each struggling to decide who should lead and who should follow. The dance music in four-four time seemed jarring to Ava. Only the waltz rhythms seemed to fit, let her glide with the music and whirl and whirl around the gym until her partners complained about getting dizzy. Ava thought, Maybe that’s why those Viennese liked it so much, it was a type of drug for them. It would become one for Ava.

In her senior year at Columbia, with a job already lined up, she moved into her Flatbush apartment, over the objections of her mother.

“You don’t have to live alone and pay rent,” her mother reasoned. “You can stay with us.”

“Mom, I’m twenty-two. Aren’t you sick of me being around? You and Pop deserve your own space.”

Her mother grinned. “Yes, you can be a pain sometimes . . . but not all the time.”

“Well, now’s your chance to do all those fun things and get the heck out of Brooklyn. I’ll be paying my own way from here on out.”

“You’ll probably make more than your father . . . but don’t ever tell him that.”

“Don’t worry, I won’t.”

Ava was glad that her mom had not bugged her about meeting men and getting married. She would not miss those embarrassing moments. Long ago she’d realized that her mother’s compliments about her grace and beauty had no relationship to the angular face and skeletal body that she stared at every morning in the mirror.

Her father helped her move in. But she stopped him after the second time he climbed six flights of stairs and looked ready to pass out. Her cousin from Jersey hauled most of the stuff upstairs on the promise that she’d buy him a case of Ballantine when they finished. Ava brought her own bed and dressers that she commandeered from her parents’ place. The apartment included some usable furniture and an old ratty rug that covered the living room floor. The rug had to go.

With much effort she pried open the window that overlooked the narrow light well. Far below, cardboard boxes, broken furniture, and even a mattress or two littered the snowy ground. Ava rolled up the rug, hauled it to the window and shoved it foot-by-foot through the opening. It unraveled on the way down, looking like some pirate’s sail, folding and flapping in the frigid wind. That first dusk she stared wide-eyed as a homeless woman staggered into the jumble of junk from the alley and covered herself with the rug. In the morning deep snow hid everything, as if the trash and the woman didn’t exist. Ava shuddered to think what the building’s Super might find come spring.

Ava found a small-time contractor to refinish the living room’s hardwood floor to a smooth glistening surface. When complete, she began her ritual of waltzing, three or four nights a week. As the country struggled to find its way out of Vietnam, as young men disappeared from the neighborhoods, as college hippies and yippies railed against The Establishment, as teargas became a known stench, as the military-industrial complex spun out of control, Ava danced.

She’d wear a simple flared skirt, drink a glass or two of wine after supper, watch the outside world’s turmoil on TV, then turn off all of the lights except for one, and waltz. Afterward, excited, her nerves buzzing, she’d shower and go to bed, touching herself, but not too much, not wanting to degrade herself or lose the mental images of dancers in huge ballrooms, of gallant men in dark evening dress, the women in long full gowns, all whirling, whirling. The dance got her there.

Every weekday morning, Ava takes the subway from Flatbush to Midtown Manhattan and her 12th-flooroffice. She’s been with the law firm now for thirty years, a competent accountant, having mastered the new computer technologies, and being promoted to section manager, in charge of budgeting. Her work relationships are all business, and although Ava gets lost in the numbers, she finds her co-workers colorless and uninteresting. She suspects they feel the same about her. 

In 1996 Ava’s father dies of a massive stroke and her mother prepares to move upstate to live with her younger sister in Utica . . . but not before criticizing Ava one last time.

“Jesus, Ava, you make good money and you’re still living in that dump. You could afford a Fifth Avenue apartment if you wanted.”

“Why would I move? You’ve lived in the same house with Pop even longer. Why didn’t you move?”

“We liked our neighbors and people knew us there, looked after your father and me when we needed help. You don’t know anybody, including your neighbors. And you never have anybody over, never—”

“Don’t start, Mother. I have what I need.”

“You mean that dance floor for one?”

“I like it like that. It’s uncomplicated and I can think whatever I want while dancing. Besides, it’s good exercise.”

Her mother grins. “I’ll give you that. You’re as skinny as ever, could pass for a twelve-year-old boy.”

“Thanks, Mom, for supporting my femininity.”

“For Christ sake, Ava, you live in a city with more than seven million people and you can’t find a single friend? What about the lady next door, Mrs. Lanchart?”

“Mom, she moved out over ten years ago. Besides, she always complained about the music.”

“I just don’t want you to give up, honey. You’re a nice person that should be with someone nice.”

“Yes, well, enjoy your train ride to Utica. Call me when you get there. I’d love to come up and visit you and Aunt Rose once you get settled.”

Ava never gets the chance. Within three weeks her mother suffers heart failure and dies within hours. Ava arranges for her to be shipped to NYC and buried in Green-Wood Cemetery, the same plot as her father and close to the grave of her Jersey cousin – killed in a car crash while driving drunk. Her parents had paid for their plot years before. It can hold one more casket. 

Her office mates express their sympathy, but it all feels like empty words. She’s been alone most of her life and is satisfied with that – at least she thinks she is.

Years pass. Ava’s auburn hair turns gray, then white. She buys a CD player then a laptop computer to play MP3 files through her speaker system that now includes quadraphonic sound. In her mid-sixties, she wraps her knees in Ace bandages before dancing and downs a Vicodin with her first glass of Riesling. The pain is bearable but it interrupts her daydreaming. She fears the time when she may have to stop and figures that’s when she’ll follow that old ratty rug out the window and add herself to the trash heap below. There were rumors that Mrs. Lanchart’s husband, Harold, did that before she moved away.

At work, Ava slows down and her bosses notice. She’s forced to take the place of a more recent hire and is tasked again with basic accounting, under a younger person’s supervision. Because of the demotion, they expect her to quit. But to their surprise, she settles in and does excellent work, giving them no reason for termination.

One night, after listening to TV news, she sips wine and prepares to dance. There’s a knock on the door, the first in a long while. Through the peephole she sees a thick-bodied man wearing glasses, with thinning dark hair and large earlobes.

“What do you want?” she calls through the door.

“Sorry to bother you, miss. You don’t know me but can I talk with you for a minute?”

“What about?”

“Your dancing.”

Ava steps back from the door. “How . . . how do you know about that?”

“I live across the light well from you. My apartment is also on the sixth floor and . . . and I can see you spin and whirl.”

“What are you, some kind of creep? A Peeping Tom?”

“No, no. Please, I mean you no disrespect. But you must know that you are a wonderful dancer, so graceful, so full of life. I’ve been watching you on Tuesdays when I’m not working the night shift at the furniture factory.”

“Why would you do that?”

“I’m not sure. I . . . I guess I need something beautiful in my life. I’ve been alone for years . . . just like you . . . have lived in this complex since ’75.”

The silence builds between them. “So . . . so what do you want?” Ava asks.

“I thought maybe we could talk and . . . and if you wouldn’t mind, let me watch you dance.”

“Look, bud, I’m not some kind of freak show for you to ogle.”

“On . . . on my word . . . I want nothing like that.”

“What’s your name?”

“Aaron Moskowitz. And yours?”

“Ava.”

“I’m glad to finally meet you, Ava. I’m kind of . . . shy.”

“Wait just a moment.” 

Ava bows her head and thinks about risks and benefits. She remembers why she took that dance class the last term in high school. She wonders if she’s still looking for physical and emotional connections, so many years later? Has all desire dried up and turned as white as her hair?

Ava unlocks the door, opens it on the chain and stares at Aaron. He smiles at her, showing off gold crowns in a broad thick-lipped mouth.

“Come back next Tuesday at eight, Aaron. And bring a bottle of chilled Riesling.”

“Any . . . any particular brand or year?”

“No, but choose wisely.”

“I have . . . and have fun checking me out online.”

“I will. Us spinsters must be extra careful.”

“Well . . . you sure can spin.”

Aaron turns and disappears from view. Ava locks the door and sits on her sofa, heart racing. She wonders why. The guy is anything but handsome and probably as graceful as a rhino. She stares around the room, sniffs the air, moves to the hall mirror and studies her gaunt reflection, her mind in scramble mode, trying to decide what to wear, how to clean the front room and bathroom, what wine glasses to set out, what music to play. Is she really going to meet this stranger? Why the hell not, she knows where he lives and his name. Not much risk. But still . . . maybe I should buy a gun?

Ava hurries to her window and looks across the courtyard to his dark apartment. As she watches, a light switches on and a hulking form moves behind see-through curtains. Her own window shade has been gone for years. Was that an unconscious act? Or was it an invitation? She smiles to herself, feeling the tingle of adventure touch her for the first time in a very long while.

Aaron Moskowitz freaks out. He wonders who that brave man was who crept along the hallways, knocked on that woman’s door, and asked if he could watch her dance. Who does that? Thinking about it now, he rushes to his apartment’s medicine cabinet and downs three antacids. But his mind continues to spin. He’ll ask Emilio at the market what Riesling is best. He’ll have his dark suit dry-cleaned and his Florsheims polished. The rest he can’t do much about; he hasn’t tried for years.

Aaron remembers summer nights when he would watch the lights in the apartment across the light well blink on. He’d open his window to hear the faint strains of music flowing from the woman’s apartment. He knew, even at first, that she listened and danced to waltzes.

The day after they met, Aaron goes online and reads up on any subject related to the waltz. He even tries to follow a simple dance lesson video that someone posted on Facebook. He doesn’t want Ava to think he’s stupid or ignorant. He scrubs hard at his stained and paint-encrusted hands, trying to remove the grunge from under his nails. He feels like a post-bar mitzvah teen waking up to the electric energy of sex and adulthood.

At precisely eight PM on Tuesday, Aaron stands outside Ava’s door and knocks – not a hammering knock, or a timid one, but something he hopes shows confidence, even though he has none. Bolts slide, chains rattle and her door opens.

“Come in . . . Aaron.”

“Thank you. I . . . I hope this is okay.” He hands her the bottle of chilled Riesling.

“I’m sure it will be fine.”

Ava wears a simple flared skirt, no jewelry or makeup, hair put up in a bun that’s pulled so tight that it looks painful to endure. Her knees are wrapped in skin-colored bandages and she wears a well-worn pair of shoes.

“You . . . you look nice, Ava,” he murmurs.

She colors slightly and nods.

“Can I pour the wine for us?” he asks.

Again, just a nod. She motions to the sofa and coffee table where two long-stemmed wine glasses and a corkscrew rest. Aaron de-corks the bottle with a flair and pours the Riesling. Ava’s first sip almost empties the glass.

She laughs. “I’m . . . I’m sorry, I haven’t had a drink with anyone since college. And never here in this apartment.”

“I’ve been drinking alone for a long time too. Not something I’m proud of.”

“So tell me the truth, Aaron, why are you here?”

“I’m still trying to figure that out. Don’t . . . don’t take this the wrong way, but if I passed you on the street I probably wouldn’t look twice. But when you dance, you can stop birds in flight . . . and I guess I’m one of ’em.”

Ava bows her head and chuckles. “I suppose that was a compliment. Thank you.”

“Sorry, I’m really nervous.” Aaron retrieves a handkerchief from an inside coat pocket and mops his expansive forehead.

“Why should you be nervous? You’re not the one dancing.”

“You’re right, you’re right.” The silence builds to an agonizing level. “So . . . so maybe you should start.”

Ava nods and moves to her laptop and queues the audio file. A sweet melody pours from the speakers. She closes her eyes and dances – nothing fancy at first, but as the music progresses, her movements become more fluid. Aaron notices that she doesn’t open her eyes at all, as if seeing the reality of her apartment and him will destroy the art. And the way she holds her imaginary partner makes him wonder what it would feel like to be with her, gliding across the polished floor.

She waltzes for almost an hour, never flagging or taking an awkward step, then sits abruptly on the sofa next to him, not speaking. They finish the bottle of wine, still silent, still wrapped up in the magic of the dance.

The silence again becomes awkward, painful. Finally, Aaron stands and struggles to find his voice. “Can . . . can I come again next Tuesday? I promise just to sit and be quiet.”

She glances sideways at him and frowns. “Well, yes, you may. But I expect you to be more social. You know, talk with me!”

“I’m sorry, I’m out of practice. Where I work, I’m in the paint booth most days and wear a mask. Not much talking going on.”

“See, that’s what I mean. Tell me something about yourself and . . . and I’ll do the same.”

Aaron grins. “I can do that. It’s a deal.”

Every Tuesday night Ava stares out her window at Aaron’s apartment, waiting for the lights to go off, a sure signal that he’s on his way. This Tuesday she is not disappointed. He arrives with the wine. They drink and talk, disclosing each week some tantalizing piece of their lives – he’s a Vietnam War veteran having served with the Airborne, she’s an expert at setting up offshore accounts for her firm’s somewhat-shady clients. Beyond biographical facts, Ava’s and Aaron’s strong emotions slowly color their conversations, exposing their disappointments, months of depression, of anger and resentment, of feeling lost, of feeling found and of happiness with their growing friendship.

This night, Ava notices that Aaron is more nervous than normal.

“Can I ask you something?” he says after taking a huge gulp of wine.

“Yes, I suppose.”

“Will you teach me to waltz . . . with you?”

She had sensed that he wanted to dance with her but has waited for him to ask, the man’s prerogative, so she’s been told.

“Yes.”

“But look, I’ve been watching you all this time and I’ve looked at online demonstration videos. I’ve practiced a little by myself.”

Ava grinned. “I don’t know much about dancing with a partner. So I’ll be a bit clumsy . . . too.”

They both empty their wine glasses. Ava queues the music and they tentatively grasp each other, his hands already wet and shaking. His whole body trembles or maybe part of it is from her. They move slowly. He stares down at his feet. She waits tensely for the first crunch of his heavy shoes on an arthritic foot, vowing not to make a sound. She’s surprised when it doesn’t happen. She keeps her eyes open and stares at his glistening face as he concentrates.

At first, dancing with Aaron feels like being moved around the room by a refrigerator. But as the weeks and months pass, she relaxes and ever so slowly Aaron becomes one of those adroit 19th-century gentlemen in evening garb, spinning her around a Vienna dance floor to a Strauss waltz. She hardly notices the pain in her knees and now her hips. But she does notice that it’s more thrilling when she keeps her eyes and heart wide open and focused on Aaron.

The touch of his right hand at the center of her back, his warm left hand grasping hers, gently now with tenderness, the spicy fragrance of his bay rum aftershave tickling her nose, the sound of his deep breathing as if in a waking dream, and the soft thud of his shoes on the hardwood floor, all excite her, make her feel, fill her life with the joy of touch, of movement, of music, of dare she admit, love.

Seasons and years pass. They both retire from their jobs yet still see each other only on Tuesday nights, the high point of Ava’s week. One Tuesday night in 2023, Ava sits at her window and stares at the rectangle of golden light that is Aaron’s apartment. Ghostly figures move behind the curtains. She glances at her watch. It’s past the time when Aaron should arrive; he’s never late. She wonders if he’s sick or maybe just sick of dancing with her and doesn’t want to do it anymore. She turns out the lights in her apartment and weeps. She knows it’s something worse.

The next day Ava talks with the Super. Aaron’s relatives have already taken the body away to someplace in White Plains. By the time she finds a phone number and contacts his younger sister, he’s already in the ground. His sister is surprised that her brother had a shiksa girlfriend and knew nothing of their Tuesday nights together.

Ava continues to dance, but only once or twice a week. Her hips are in bad shape, painful, and she uses a cane. The sound of its soft thud on the hardwood floor reminds her of Aaron and his Florsheims, plodding along. She dances now with her eyes wide open and all the lights turned on, but with the memory of a real dance partner to carry her forward.

32 pieces, 32 writers, one theme: what it costs to be seen, and what it costs not to be.

We are watched and don’t know it. We wait to be recognized and are not. When we are noticed, we learn it carries a cost of its own.

The 32 writers range from first publication to fifty years of it, and each arrived at this question on their own.

We didn’t build the issue around it. The issue told us what it was, and we recognized it.

Welcome to the inaugural edition of Inkhorn Review, September 2026.

tags.name: Terry Sanville
tags.description: Terry Sanville lives in San Luis Obispo, California with his artist-poet wife (his in-house editor) and two plump cats (his in-house critics). His short stories have been accepted more than 600 times by journals, magazines, and anthologies. Terry is a retired urban planner and an accomplished jazz and blues guitarist.

html:
I did not save it.
That’s the first truth.

It stood in the road
with one wing folded wrong,
black lacquer split along the bone.

It watched me
with an eye that knows I,
that understands traffic,
that has learned what human means.

It slowed.
I could have reached.
The space between us
was not large.

But the crow did not beg.

It did not scatter.

It did not challenge itself
to flee.

It held its ground
like something that already decided.

I thought of hands.

Of lifting.

The way angels do
in stories stiff in hide and faith.

The car behind me inhaled.

The road argued with the brake.

The day kept going.

So I stayed.

Behind the car,
feathers lifted,
no shadow, no cry,
no sudden absolution.

Only later did I feel it:
the weight of having chosen
nothing remarkable.

Crows remember faces.

They carry debts.

They gather in mourning.

If it calls me back,
I will not pretend I know it not.

I knew
what I was doing
when I kept my feet
still to the road.

html:
Yaya sits at her coffee table focusing where red blurs of watercolor and blue splatters of the sky meet on a glass bowl and I can tell she’s not quite here, the silence broken by an occasional wave, she begins to speak.

Did you know that sea glass are mermaids' tears that shed when they fall in love with a mortal man that’s someone else's? It's romantic," she says, "Sacrifice means love, and to love means to give oneself up in every manner. That's how you capture a mermaid.”

“To give yourself to a mermaid, the tide must be lower than that peach pit in your stomach. Only then should you walk across the sandbars and find where the tide will swallow you. Let yourself float down as waves crash across your velvet flesh pushing into your bones. Breathe, breathe, letting the salt water stain you. When your vision blanks ears popping from the pressure, you'll see the first tail, then the eyes snake towards you. Rows of scales brush the soles of your feet, and in the dark waves they're watching to see how easily you give up.”

“They'll circle you. Watching. Waiting for Moirai to cut your thread.”

“Only then, when the snip sounds and you thud against the bottom, where Apollo can’t see, the pressure folds you up. Spine ripped out of your back by the nails of the one you loved. Then go your eyes, followed by muscles, lastly sinews become fish feed. Bones, however, are pressed smooth and flat by the pressure –”

I find myself interrupting. "But why is sea glass so smooth, Yaya, and where did Pappou go all those years ago?"

"He's right here, darling," Grandma responds. She reaches above me with a yellow tinged nail and taps on the cloudy red and blue glass bowl that sounds much more hollow than it does glass.

html:
You are now in awe
Of its power, this faded blue rag
You are ripping
To mop up a spill -
A jacket you saw
Last on shoulders fast learning to sag
In the nipping
Winter, poised and chill,
In work-worn hands
Robbed of their last dream.

The piece of cloth lands
Like a gut-punch -
Makes you remember,
And makes you hunch
Your own shoulders;
You tear asunder
What never was whole.

The sharp sound,
The film of dust, rising
From the wound
In one final burst of glory
Is a funeral-rite
In no lore for a memory:

This will resurrect
Itself; return, bristling,
Reach for another bite
Of your sanity -
Resurrect, and bracket
Itself squarely in a thing
Ripe to meet its fate -
A chipped plate,
A creaking swing-set,
Another jean-jacket.

tags.name: Autumn 2026
tags.description:
32 pieces, 32 writers, one theme: what it costs to be seen, and what it costs not to be.

We are watched and don’t know it. We wait to be recognized and are not. When we are noticed, we learn it carries a cost of its own.

The 32 writers range from first publication to fifty years of it, and each arrived at this question on their own.

We didn’t build the issue around it. The issue told us what it was, and we recognized it.

Welcome to the inaugural edition of Inkhorn Review, September 2026.

tags.name: Hibah Shabkhez
tags.description: Hibah Shabkhez is a writer and photographer from Lahore, Pakistan. Her work has previously appeared in Arc Poetry, Meniscus, Thimble, Harpur Palate, and a number of other literary magazines. Studying life, languages, and literature from a comparative perspective across linguistic and cultural boundaries holds a particular fascination for her.

We scrambled off our cots simultaneously and stared blankly toward the door.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“Who’s there?” Mom asked.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“I’m here to repossess your car, ma’am.”","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“It doesn’t even have air conditioning,” she said. ","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"That didn’t influence the voice on the other side of the door.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“Ma’am, I’m just doing my job. I shoved him hard. ","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“What are you afraid of, you pretty little thing?” he said as he twirled a strand of my hair around his index finger and placed it behind my ear.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":" “Leave her alone, Ray!” Mom shouted.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I stood upright on the bed and leapt into Sam’s sanctuary a scant foot away, but it seemed much farther.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Mom picked up a hairbrush from the side table and pointed it at Ray. ","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“One way or another, we’re leaving day after tomorrow,” she said. “Now get out of here, you bastard.”","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"True to her word this time, we flew back to Miami two days later, arriving well before the check bounced.
