He gave Mom a big hug; she didn’t hug him back, but she didn’t pull away, either.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I’d missed more than a month of school, and when I showed up the first day, I was told that I’d missed too many days and would have to repeat tenth grade. I’m not sure how Mom did it, but she convinced the principal that I would ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":2,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"not ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"be repeating any grades. As I sat on a bench outside the office, my fingers touching an engraved somebody hearts somebody, I overheard her say, “Over my dead body.” And that was that. ","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":3,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Miami","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Crawling out of poverty is a steep climb, but, little by little, we made progress. When I turned fifteen, I began working after school at Burdine’s Department Store’s warehouse stapling price tags on clothing. When I turned sixteen, I worked at their store in the mall. Other places I worked as a teen included Arthur Treacher’s Fish and Chips and an ice cream parlor. All these jobs paid minimum wage, but the fact that I was earning money made me feel like a million dollars. ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":2,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"And ","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I received discounts on clothing, fried fish and chips, and ice cream. ","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Mom landed a job as a medical secretary at Jackson Memorial Hospital and met my stepfather there. I started college when I was eighteen and benefited from government aid in the form of college work-study programs and scholarships, then was awarded a teaching fellowship for my master’s degree. ","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Still, there’s no question that poverty left its mark. The things that poverty robbed me of, at least for a time, included my self-esteem, sense of security, and, maybe more importantly, my identity. I had to abandon my child’s self when we left West Virginia; I was forced to grow up way too quickly and craft a new self in order to survive.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Although I now enjoy a relatively stable and secure life, poverty blocked my light source long enough to form a shadow that always hovers nearby. I’m still anxious about going hungry; I can’t look at a Krispy Kreme Doughnut box, let alone eat a doughnut. They bring back memories of the first time I realized there was no longer any real food on the table. There are days when I feel that the life I’ve built might be snatched away at any moment; after all, it happened before.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I’m grateful for the things I carried with me that lay beyond the robber’s reach. Among them, my love of reading, motivated by that bus full of books that visited my small town twice a week, inspiring me to dream about life’s possibilities; my determination to excel in school to prove that I wasn’t dumb like the California kids thought, leading to my college scholarships; and my ability to sort out and write down thoughts in the little white diary, giving me the courage to tell my story. ","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Poverty robbed me of many things, but the itinerant thief failed to steal that which nourished my heart and my soul.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
html:
Growing up in a small Appalachian town in the 1960s, I didn’t feel poor. Daddy had a job at a chemical plant down in Charleston, and we always had food on the table. We wore decent clothes and shoes, hand-me-downs for sure, but if anything needed mending, Mom sat down at her Singer sewing machine and made it as good as new, well almost, in no time. 

We couldn’t afford to buy a house; we were perpetual renters, but we always had a roof over our heads. No, we weren’t poor. The poor people lived back in the hollers; some of the kids from there showed up at school looking a bit scruffy, but no one teased them. Safely cloaked by a grandma shawl of hills and mountains, we all shared a strong sense of place.

If my sisters or I needed to see a doctor or have our eyes examined, Mom drove us twenty miles down to Charleston. If I wanted to read a book, and I read lots of them, I visited the bookmobile that came to town a couple times a week. 

We didn’t take vacations, unless you considered Vacation Bible School one, and we didn’t eat at restaurants, unless you put Dairy Queen in that category. The rental houses we lived in were mostly rundown, some had issues with rodents, I always shared a bedroom with one of my sisters, Mel, the oldest, or Sam, the youngest, and our furniture was old and beat up. I remember Mom using her artistic talents to try and raise the standards in each house we lived in. She and my grandmother made curtains and hung them from one end of the living room to the other, making it appear that there must be a large picture window behind them. There wasn’t; just two regular windows that didn’t close properly and allowed the cold air to seep in during the winter. At the time, I didn’t realize what a no-frills life it was, but we were better off than many.

California

When I was in my early teens, Mom traded the sewing machine for the stage. She’d always had a dramatic flair and starred in musicals and plays at the local “theatre,” also known as the Clendenin High School auditorium. But she wanted more; specifically, she wanted to become Doris Day, or at least as famous. A series of events put that dream in play, at least for a while. My grandmother, whom we called “Artie,” had moved to California in the early 1950s to live with her sister. Divorced from my grandfather, she was eight months pregnant with a baby whose father was a married man. She gave the baby up for adoption, which is what women did in those days, and, soon after, remarried. 

Artie was always egging Mom on to leave that “hell hole,” which is how she referred to West Virginia, so by the time she visited from California, Mom had already divorced my father and met Ray, a man she thought had money. Ray moved us into a rental house near Charleston, close to where he lived, meaning my sisters and I had to change schools. My sense of safety and security began to erode; the erosion and weathering that had taken hundreds of millions of years to create West Virginia’s beautiful mountains, began to form a new me, rather quickly. We’d lived there a few months when we received an eviction notice. Ray said there must be some mistake, but he supported the idea of our moving to California. 

Mom woke us up early one autumn morning.

“You can only take what’ll fit into the trunk,” she said. “Don’t dilly-dally . . . figure out what’s important.” 

“We should all get the same amount of space,” Mel said. I was surprised she didn’t lobby for more.

No matter how many times I calculated it, I ended up with five feet of total trunk space, divided by five people, which equaled a foot of space per person. My math skills were impeccable. 

I packed my majorette’s uniform, my Holy Bible with Helps, and my little white diary, officially, into the trunk. At the last minute, I smuggled my baton and favorite game, Mousetrap, into an empty space I spotted behind Mom’s hot pink Samsonite overnight bag, near the spare tire. 

Mom gunned the V-gazillion engine on our brand-new 1965 Blue Impala convertible that she purchased the week before—I don’t think she used green stamps—and we headed west to fulfill her dream of becoming Doris Day. Mel, Sam and I shared the backseat, and Artie rode shotgun, frequently wielding her Vicks Inhaler stick, each nostril indulged by two quick sniffs. Afterwards, she slid the tube back down into the middle part of her bra, where it rested inside ample cleavage. She said she kept it there so she wouldn’t misplace it. Luckily, she wasn’t a hugger. Still, the pungent, menthol odor cleared our ten sinuses collectively within seconds, leaving no doubt that we were riding in a new car. 

Ray stayed behind to “finish up some business” but said he’d come out, soon. After three long days on the road, we arrived in California and moved into Artie and her husband’s small apartment, which they shared with Luigi, a beer-sipping parrot. Although the living arrangements were tight, Mom emphasized that it was only temporary until Ray arrived. Then, we’d move into a bigger house, and she could follow her dreams. In the meantime, we still had a roof over our heads, food on the table thanks to Tony, my step-grandfather, as well as clothes and shoes, but since we’d left most of our belongings back home with Aunt Jean, our wardrobe choices were slim.

The almost three-thousand-mile journey was littered along the way with figments of my imagination, which hadn’t yet been forged into my own dreams. I focused on the things I’d left behind—my dog, my friends, all the places imprinted on the map of my child’s mind, including the Roxy movie theater where I saw To Kill a Mockingbird and someone commented that I looked like Scout Finch on the movie poster; Cemetery Hill, where I had a front-row seat at its bottom as the dead were carted up the steep mountain road by the Blackwell’s, the family who owned the local funeral home; the Elk River, our muddy beach, which might as well have been the ocean on a hot summer day; and the bookmobile, perhaps my favorite place of all, where I checked out books and read about far-away places, never imagining I’d ever visit one.

Then came the first day of school, ninth grade for me. The California kids teased me about my Appalachian drawl, called me Elly May Clampett, asked me if I could read, and stared at me as if I were an alien dropped from the sky. This is when I began to realize that maybe I was poor, and dumb.

Luckily, or maybe not, within a few months, we left California for Miami, where Ray said he would meet us—he claimed he had contacts there—and we’d move into a big house with plenty of bedrooms and a swimming pool.

Miami

We exited I-95 onto Ali Baba Avenue in Opa-locka, Florida, essentially a slum north of Miami. Everyone was quiet, until Mom spoke.

“Look for Scheherazade Boulevard. You know, like in Ali Baba and the 

Forty Thieves.” 

We turned onto Scheherazade. A gilt-trimmed six-foot wall flanked by domed turrets attached at each end shielded the front of the Ali Baba Efficiency Apartments. The bright sun reflected off the wall, causing us to shade our eyes. Sam asked if the wall contained real gold.

“Open Sesame,” Sam said.

“Open Sesame,” I said. I hadn’t totally given up on the idea that some things that glittered really were gold. 

We entered through the broken gate, which was already open, and encountered a one-story, pink stucco building with twenty or so “apartments” horseshoed around a courtyard. 

 “Garden apartment,” Mom said. 

I didn’t see any garden, and, not to be picky, but it looked more like a rundown motel to me.

We pulled into parking space number seven, next to the biggest pink Cadillac I’d ever seen. True, it had dents and bangs all over every inch of its exterior and was rusty as an old nail, but, still, it was a Cadillac, a pink one. 

“Don’t just sit there,” Mom said. “Let’s get this stuff inside.”

She pulled out what looked like a skeleton key to open the door. At one end of the tiny two-room “apartment” was a kitchenette with cracked and buckled linoleum, a small gas stove with a slick film of grease on its surface, a refrigerator and a dinette set. The small table was covered with a plastic tablecloth depicting faded flowers I couldn’t name. Its four mismatched chairs had one thing in common, straight backs that didn’t allow for slumping. 

The white refrigerator, short and squat with a rounded belly and a shiny, chrome, fin-shaped handle, reminded me of Casper the Friendly Ghost. But inside it was dark and empty, more like one of the mean ghosts who taunted and teased Casper.

In the other room, four cots were lined up military style, one for each of us. This arrangement was perfect for those times when I pretended to be Clara Barton or Florence Nightingale caring for wounded war heroes. I imagined keeping the soldiers as comfortable as possible during their final days. 

A boxy 1966 Zenith color TV rested on pointy legs in the middle of the room—fat ballerina came to mind. I bent down to inspect the television a little closer. One of the rabbit ears was bent to the side. 

“Well,” I said, pointing to the antenna, “that means it’ll be snowing in Florida while we watch The Wonderful World of Disney.” 

“Snowing?” Sam asked. “Does it snow in Florida?”

I gently ribbed her with my elbow. “No, but when the reception on a TV isn’t good, the picture has white speckles, what they call snowy. Get it?” 

The only two windows, one in the kitchen and the other in the barracks, as I referred to it, were covered by thick, white vinyl shades that didn’t allow much light in. In fact, it could have been the middle of the day, and nobody would have called me crazy had I placed my hand on my little Holy Bible with Helps and sworn it was nighttime.

“It’s furnished,” Mom said.

I staked out the cot nearest the front window; the air conditioner was broken.

Many days after school, I sat in one of the orphaned chairs in the kitchen reading Gone with the Wind, a big, heavy, green hardcover I checked out of the school library. I rested it on my lap and read for hours, only changing positions to pry my sweaty legs loose from the chair’s hard, cracked vinyl seat. Mom cooked around me. My sisters watched TV or argued.

“That’s a big book you’re reading,” Mom said.

“I guess.”

“We won’t be here much longer.” 

I had learned that Mom’s sense of time was much different than my own.

“What are you cooking?” I asked.

“Beans and cornbread, your favorite.”

I already knew the answer. The heavy odor of grease from the bacon she used to flavor the beans clung to my clothes and probably everyone else’s within two miles. The exhaust fan on the stove was broken, too. 

Many nights, Mom went outside to a common area of the Ali Baba to use the payphone. I knew she was calling Ray and asking him when he’d be down, when we’d be moving into that nice house he promised her. She’d come back inside and say, “Soon.”

One evening in October, someone knocked on the door while we were watching TV. The brass eagle knocker had a broken beak, which I only thought about when someone used it. They rarely did, except to collect the rent. We scrambled off our cots simultaneously and stared blankly toward the door.

“Who’s there?” Mom asked.

“I’m here to repossess your car, ma’am.”

“It doesn’t even have air conditioning,” she said. 

That didn’t influence the voice on the other side of the door.

“Ma’am, I’m just doing my job. I’ll give you five minutes to get any personal belongings out.”

As Mom opened the door, she turned to us. “Don’t just sit there, see if there’s anything in the car you want.”

Mel, Sam and I slinked out to the Blue Impala. I opened the glove compartment, and the tiny light revealed official-looking papers and our well-worn map of the United States. 

“Put everything in this garbage bag,” Mom said, furling it open. 

Next, I ran my hand along the back of the fluted vinyl bucket seats and reached into the dead space where the seat backs connected to the seats themselves. I found five pennies, a gum wrapper, and one of Artie’s Vick’s Inhaler sticks. Mel and Sam stayed busy in the back seat conducting their own treasure hunt. 

As I extended my arm into the darkness under the front seat and pulled out an empty Coke bottle, a memory flashed through my mind. During our journey from California to Florida, I fixated on the image of a real impala in the center of the steering wheel, a sleek and graceful African antelope that could leap up to heights of ten feet; I learned about it from reading the introduction in the owner’s manual. Staring at it calmed me; I could focus on it instead of Mom’s tired eyes, which I couldn’t help but notice when she glanced in the rearview mirror. 

Now, I lay down the booty from under the seats, spit on my right palm and rubbed it on the image of the African impala.

“Leap for luck always,” I said. 

The man averted his eyes, whether out of respect or disgust, I didn’t know.

Mom stooped down next to the right rear tire. A strange sound followed. “Ssssshhhhhh!”

The man jumped and ran toward the noise.

“What are you doing, ma’am?”

By the time the man moved around to where Mom was, it was already too late, at least for that tire. She stabbed it repeatedly with a tarnished butcher knife from the kitchen drawer, and I prayed the landlord wasn’t watching. 

“Her patience is wearing thin,” I said. “You’d better get going.”

It was November, and we left the windows open at night to catch a breeze. Tenants talked and laughed outside, and the now familiar odors of cigarette smoke and alcohol mixed and climbed into bed with me, making my stomach queasy. If I hadn’t known better, I would have sworn that Ray was standing right outside our door. I peeked out the window and saw some middle-aged men who looked down on their luck, sitting on white plastic chairs laughing up a storm, a little more than I thought was appropriate under the circumstances. 

I lay awake and wondered why these “apartments” were called efficiencies. One answer that came to me was that they were efficient for people who were in between, a rest stop to sort things out before they started living their lives again. My rest stop was reading. 

Mom worked three jobs—counter waitress at Krispy Kreme Doughnuts, waitress at Wolfie’s Delicatessen, and elevator operator at the Fontainebleau Hotel—to pay the rent and put whatever food she could afford on the table. Thankfully, two of the jobs provided culinary benefits. She brought home leftover doughnuts from Krispy Kreme; I usually ate an original glaze for breakfast and a chocolate cream-filled for dessert. We also received a discount at Wolfie’s; the pastrami sandwiches were great. 

Now that the car had been repossessed, our only form of transportation was by bus; that is until Bob Johnson, the manager of Krispy Kreme, started dating Mom. He took us to Publix once a week or so to buy real food. I could tell Mom didn’t like him, but she put up with him for a while, mainly I think for the enhanced culinary benefits.

One day, after Mom had gone on a rant about not being able to afford to pay the bills, we took the bus to the United Way office to ask for assistance. My sisters and I waited outside. She returned an hour later, tears streaming down her face. 

“They said we don’t quality for assistance!” she screamed.

I remember thinking, if we don’t, then who does?

On Thanksgiving, Mom went to the horse track with Bob. When she got home, she was carrying a sixteen-pound turkey she had won at a raffle there. 

“Happy Thanksgiving,” she said, and plopped the turkey on the dinette table. “Let’s eat!”

Luckily, it was already cooked; the oven had recently died.

After we moved out of the Pink Palace, which is what I called the Ali Baba, we lived in a variety of apartments and rundown houses in the Miami area, one situated right behind Krispy Kreme. Artie had come to visit, so for a while—she didn’t take short trips—there were five of us living there. Sam claimed the solo bedroom because her bad headaches had returned. The other bedroom, with one twin bed, was billed as first come, first served. 

The three stragglers ended up sleeping on yellow nylon-banded lounge chairs in the living room. I had made a couple of friends at school and didn’t want to show up with striped indentations on my face and legs from the lounge chairs, so I went to bed early. To their credit, Mom, Artie and Mel didn’t seem to mind. Many nights, they lay on the lounge chairs talking and laughing as if they were on some beach having the time of their lives. The only thing missing were those fancy drinks with little umbrellas.

I was beginning to understand that we were going to need a lot more than luck to get out of our increasingly dire situation. And roof over our heads or not, I felt homeless.

West Virginia

Summer arrived, and Mom sent me and my sisters back up to West Virginia by Greyhound Bus to visit Daddy, his wife and their daughter. Mom was back in a relationship with Ray, who turned out not to be rich, but he wasn’t poor, either. 

Mom and Ray picked us up on a hot August morning. We were inside getting our stuff together and saying goodbye to Daddy when we heard the horn. Ray sat behind the wheel of his white Cadillac, not making a move to get out and help. Mom got out, gave us each a tired hug, and opened the trunk. It was much roomier than the Blue Impala’s, but we’d already chosen what was most important a couple years earlier, based on the size of the smaller trunk, so the extra space wasn’t needed. As I climbed into the back seat, I wondered who was riding in the Blue Impala, now. 

“So, we’re headed back to Florida,” Mel said, more to break the awkward silence. 

“Well, not quite yet,” Mom said. “Ray’s got a few final things he needs to take care of, so we’re going to stay in a motel for a couple of days. It has tennis courts.”

I had no clue why tennis courts were significant; none of us had ever played a day in our lives. Their mention, however, briefly added a sense of glamour to the place, until I saw it. The Dunbar Inn, in Dunbar, West Virginia, was like a Holiday Inn without any hint of a holiday. We checked into a room with two double beds. Ray stayed somewhere else.  

“It’ll just be a couple of days,” Mom said after he left. 

“But what’ll we do here?” Mel asked. “We don’t have a car anymore.” She had a valid point for a change.

“Learn to play tennis,” Mom said.

Sam and I borrowed the old rackets they kept behind the front desk and hit tennis balls around on the court. Mel fumed inside. Mom perfected her waiting game. A week later, after it became clear that Mom’s couple of days still had their own unique meaning, Mel flew back to Miami to start her first year of college on scholarship. She’d received the notice right before we left Florida and would temporarily live with Artie’s sister.

With Mel gone, it was just Sam and me, a nine-year-old and a fourteen-year-old left to our own devices in a rundown motel.

In addition to her headaches and night screams, Sam had started to behave strangely in other ways, including twirling around inside the room until she got dizzy and fell. All the recent changes in our lives had caught up with her, and she seemed untethered from reality. We’d given up on tennis for the most part; it was too hot out, and neither of us got any satisfaction from hitting a ball back and forth over a net. Our new favorite pastime was watching TV. I would have preferred to read a book, but we had no car to get to the library, and Mom was nervous about the fact that we weren’t in school. Still, she said, “Only a couple more days.” 

Sam and I loved the new show on CBS called It’s About Time; it featured two astronauts who had broken the time barrier and ended up in prehistoric times. My favorite part was the theme song that began, “It’s about time, it’s about space, about strange people in the strangest place.” After watching several episodes, I sang along one night.     

With a pencil for a microphone, I belted the words, “It’s about time.”

Sam’s face beamed. She jumped up and down on the bed and shouted, “I want to go to the strangest place!”

 “Stop screaming, Sam,” Mom said. “You girls go downstairs to the motel restaurant and order something good for dinner.”

“Last time, they asked me to tell you that we owe for two weeks rent, plus the motel restaurant food,” I said.

“You tell them we’ll be paying soon.”

I was embarrassed, but I was hungry, too. 

“We’d like to order, please.” Sam stood next to me, staring at the floor.

“I’m sorry, girls, but you’ll have to tell your mom that we can’t give you any more food until the bill is paid in full. I’m really sorry.” 

That evening, the three of us walked a mile or so to the nearest grocery store. Along the way, Mom stopped at every payphone and searched for coins that someone may have left in the refund chute; she only had about ten dollars in her pocketbook. While we were in the peanut butter aisle, I whispered, “It’s About Time” in Sam’s ear, and she started jumping up and down screaming, “I want to go to the strangest place.” I didn’t know she’d pull the same stunt outside the room, but I didn’t know she wouldn’t, either. I was becoming a bit untethered, too. I was scared and hungry.

We returned with peanut butter, crackers, sugar cubes, marshmallows, and milk. The marshmallows were a bribe to get Sam to shut up. Not exactly the five major food groups, but Mom said it was only for a couple more days.

By the middle of September, we’d been living at the motel for a month. Ray came and went. One of those times when Ray appeared, Mom finally started pressing him.

“Ray, the girls were supposed to start school a month ago.” 

“You got money?” Ray said, pointing his finger at Mom in a taunting way. “Fly back.”

Mom pointed to the dresser where we’d made a makeshift kitchen and lined up our rations. 

“You know I don’t have any money! Why do you think we’re eating peanut butter and sugar cubes?” 

As he walked out the door, Ray angrily said, “I’m doing this for you. This is a big construction deal I’m working on, worth lots of money.” 

“Why don’t we call Daddy,” I said. “We could go back there and stay.”

“No!” Mom said.

Minutes later, there was a knock at the door. No one knew we were there except Ray, and he had a key.

“Who’s there?” Mom asked.

“County School Officer,” a gruff voice replied.

Mom slowly opened the door, and the owner of the gruff voice stood there waiting to be invited in. He scanned the room.

“May I come in?” 

Mom opened the door wider and the officer stepped inside. She sat down on the bed, and I sat next to her. Sam stayed in the background, watching.

“We have a report that you have two children here who aren’t attending school.”

“We live in Florida; we’re going back soon. My husband has business here.”

Mom must have thought that saying Ray was her husband would carry more weight. We found out much later that he was already married to someone else.

“Well, you need to get these girls in school.” He didn’t say this unkindly, but it was clear he meant business.

Looking back, I’m not sure if it was the school officer’s visit or Ray’s later that night that got us out of the Dunbar Inn, maybe a little of both. Sam lay in the bed on the far side of the room. Mom and I sat with our heads propped up on pillows watching TV in the other bed closest to the door. The sweet, pungent odor of liquor entered the room first, followed by Ray. Alcohol made Daddy sleepy; it made Ray mean. 

“How exciting, you’re watching Jeopardy,” he said. He crawled into the bed between Mom and me and started sloppy kissing her. 

I stiffened but didn’t move. “I was here first,” I said. 

Ray started tickling me with his fat fingers; I shoved him hard. 

“What are you afraid of, you pretty little thing?” he said as he twirled a strand of my hair around his index finger and placed it behind my ear.

 “Leave her alone, Ray!” Mom shouted.

I stood upright on the bed and leapt into Sam’s sanctuary a scant foot away, but it seemed much farther.

Mom picked up a hairbrush from the side table and pointed it at Ray. 

“One way or another, we’re leaving day after tomorrow,” she said. “Now get out of here, you bastard.”

True to her word this time, we flew back to Miami two days later, arriving well before the check bounced. Bob picked us up at the airport. He gave Mom a big hug; she didn’t hug him back, but she didn’t pull away, either.

I’d missed more than a month of school, and when I showed up the first day, I was told that I’d missed too many days and would have to repeat tenth grade. I’m not sure how Mom did it, but she convinced the principal that I would not be repeating any grades. As I sat on a bench outside the office, my fingers touching an engraved somebody hearts somebody, I overheard her say, “Over my dead body.” And that was that. 

Miami

Crawling out of poverty is a steep climb, but, little by little, we made progress. When I turned fifteen, I began working after school at Burdine’s Department Store’s warehouse stapling price tags on clothing. When I turned sixteen, I worked at their store in the mall. Other places I worked as a teen included Arthur Treacher’s Fish and Chips and an ice cream parlor. All these jobs paid minimum wage, but the fact that I was earning money made me feel like a million dollars. And I received discounts on clothing, fried fish and chips, and ice cream. 

Mom landed a job as a medical secretary at Jackson Memorial Hospital and met my stepfather there. I started college when I was eighteen and benefited from government aid in the form of college work-study programs and scholarships, then was awarded a teaching fellowship for my master’s degree. 

Still, there’s no question that poverty left its mark. The things that poverty robbed me of, at least for a time, included my self-esteem, sense of security, and, maybe more importantly, my identity. I had to abandon my child’s self when we left West Virginia; I was forced to grow up way too quickly and craft a new self in order to survive.

Although I now enjoy a relatively stable and secure life, poverty blocked my light source long enough to form a shadow that always hovers nearby. I’m still anxious about going hungry; I can’t look at a Krispy Kreme Doughnut box, let alone eat a doughnut. They bring back memories of the first time I realized there was no longer any real food on the table. There are days when I feel that the life I’ve built might be snatched away at any moment; after all, it happened before.

I’m grateful for the things I carried with me that lay beyond the robber’s reach. Among them, my love of reading, motivated by that bus full of books that visited my small town twice a week, inspiring me to dream about life’s possibilities; my determination to excel in school to prove that I wasn’t dumb like the California kids thought, leading to my college scholarships; and my ability to sort out and write down thoughts in the little white diary, giving me the courage to tell my story. 

Poverty robbed me of many things, but the itinerant thief failed to steal that which nourished my heart and my soul.

html:
“Nothing”
is a failure in observation
brought on, at times,
by the deflated hopes
of the eager in waiting

as if the honey-colored tea
filling the glass cup
on the oaken surface of a table
were to suddenly take the stage
and explain
its bright and gory origins,

of how it was plucked,
green-leafed and oblivious
from under a glowing sun,
then rootless, might have wished
to wander, but instead withered,
shoulder-to-shoulder
with the most aromatic
but unintelligible of companions.

I will spare you
the parts about chopping, darkness,
damp pungency, so you, too,
will brighten when you remember
again the cup, the honey-colored tea
when you say nothing.

html:
It had been a miserable year. My wife finally left me after screwing around with a guy she met while working on a publicity gig, thinking I didn’t know. Having done the same thing during the first years of our marriage, I was well aware of the signs and the first whiff put me on my guard. 

It was the night she told me she had to work late and left me a shrimp casserole—my absolute favorite food—in the fridge to heat up for my dinner, explaining in a note that she didn’t know what time she would be home. When I was involved in a fuckin’ hot affaire, I hadn’t left anything for her to chew on...except suspicion.

Did I tell her I knew that she wasn’t working? Of course I didn’t. Do you think I’m stupid? I wanted her to leave more signs until she was so involved that there was no way for her to excuse herself. But I hadn’t anticipated—or planned—for her to simply get up and leave...and not even a shrimp casserole to console me. Inconsiderate, that’s what it was.

I called our kids to tell them what their mother had done, but all I got was silence. I didn’t leave a message; what for? They would only side with their mother, calling me an asshole for having done the same thing to her, that I deserved her walking out on me.

I called her mother. Despite being my mother-in-law, we had always had a good relationship. She was fair, never taking sides. Something must have been wrong with her phone line because all I got was static. 

I called my own mother, but then remembered that she was on a cruise around the world and might be asleep, so I hung up before it went to voicemail. 

I was restless. I needed to confess to someone how I felt.

“I was hoping you would come,” Adele greeted me as I walked in. 

“I was miserable,” I told her.

“Staying late at the office can be a drag...especially when there’s nothing that is so urgent that you feel you must,” she said, offering me a whiskey on ice.

“Yeah, it can be an excuse,” I said, taking the drink and sitting on the sofa.

“Well, Henry, you can always count on me to have the solution.”  I followed her into the kitchen and sat at the kitchen table set for two, watching her as she took a casserole out of the oven.

“Shrimp, your favorite,” setting the dish in front of me. 

“You’re so good to me, Adele.”

“Henry, you always seem surprised.”

“I always am. How many wives know exactly how their husbands feel and what will get them out of their depressed state,” I said.

“Now, don’t tell me you phoned our kids, my mother, and your mother, because you know we never had children, my mother died 15 years ago, and your mother never answers her phone. I think you do all this because you know I’ll bake your favorite food for dinner when you tell me you’ll be staying late at the office. Now let’s eat; I’m starved.”

html:
I went to two old high schools in
my Carolina town.
The one was home to white students,
the other home to brown.
The old white school was girded by
the nicest homes around.
The black school had a graveyard by
the playground. And a cow.

","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"When the ball has dropped, when the neighbors have left, when all the hot chocolate has been drunk, and the artist tipped handsomely, Sophie lures Andrew to her web.         ","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"type":"horizontalrule","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Seeking more, more, more, they push the boundaries of what they thought they knew. html:
Birthday parties are as inevitable as death and taxes, in his line of work.

Today, the balloons are bright and the sky is reflective and the kids are screaming and the cake is wilting under the heat and the kids are still screaming. Hundreds of them. No, that’s an exaggeration. Dozens, then. 

The face paint on Andrew’s cheek is mildly claustrophobic, too — its clamminess heavy as the artist continues to add layers. So, Andrew breathes in. Breathes out. Swallows past the smell of sugar and pepperoni and overheating bounce house plastic. He looks for his wife, who ditched him a half hour ago. 

They’d expressly agreed Not to Ditch Each Other and to head out once the cake was cut. But, these parties have a way of drawing people apart. Now, Sophie is standing 40 feet to his right, just out of reach of the shade and his pleas. 

She smiles and nods to another mom, all while swaying under the onslaught of preschoolers threatening to take her out at the knee. He would say she deserves it, but he loves her. 

He, meanwhile, is balancing on a too-small chair while his son watches. 

“Handsome, Daddy,” his 4-year-old son beams, ants in his pants. The very son who convinced him to visit the face painting tent. 

“All done,” the artist says, handing him a mirror. “What do you think?” 

That I look like an asshole. “It’s great,” he responds before even seeing his reflection. Then, he catches a glimpse. “I . . .” He turns his head this way, that way. Rolls his neck. Straightens his shoulders. Andrew had pointed to the first sample picture on the board in the face painting tent, and now…

“You a prince, Daddy!” 

He supposes he is. He offers the artist a smile and the mirror, and she curtsies. Her cheeks flush pink.   

Andrew stands from the chair, his back ramrod. He takes measured steps toward his wife. His son bounces at his heels.  

“Looking good, Andrew,” shouts a passerby. 

Andrew dips his head, then continues his promenade across the yard. 

He reaches his wife and, instinctually, she welcomes him with a hand to his forearm. Then double-takes. 

“Andy,” she breathes, a nervous giggle hidden in her words. “You? Where have you been?” She sounds as if she’s just run a mile, her chest rising and falling. Her gaze sweeps his face, then settles on his eyes. 

“Oh, I . . .” 

The other woman interjects: “You have to share your skincare routine. You look about 10 years younger than the last time I saw you. Glowing.” She exhales, a hand to her chest. 

Andrew squints and purses his lips, unsure if she’s being facetious. “What do I use, babe?” he asks his wife. 

Sophie doesn’t take her eyes off him. “Just this stuff I saw on TikTok. I can send you a link.” Then to Andrew: “You do look . . . different. More . . .” 

“Well, I’m royalty now, so, yeah?” 

“Yeah?” She shakes the question from her head. 

As soon as the other woman leaves, Sophie reaches up on tip toes to whisper in his ear. “You’re so handsome, Andy. I don’t think I tell you that enough.”     

The party continues with the usual beats — games, pizza, presents – but he relaxes into it. The other parents make their way over one-by-one to say hello. He waves a hand. Nods his head. Entertains their greetings. 

And true to their word, Andrew, Sophie, and the children leave promptly after cake, Sophie’s arm linked with Andrew’s all the way to the car, like they’re newlyweds again. He waits until the kids are buckled in then kisses her against the hatchback. He wipes a smudge of blue paint from her cheek before climbing into the car himself.

This weekend, the party is for his seven-year-old daughter’s friend, so there are considerably fewer dinosaurs and substantially more tiaras. Andrew watches his daughter get a unicorn horn swiped across her freckled forehead, the pinks amalgamating. 

He asks if it’d be ok if he had a turn. If there are no kids waiting, of course. It’s just for fun. 

This artist acquiesces with a smirk, and Andrew tells her what he’d like. When he peers into the mirror five minutes later and sees the red and black paint of a superhero, his muscles flex themselves. Sophie steps up behind him and traces her fingers across the small of his back. 

“When did you start working out again?” she teases with a smile and a squeeze on his defined shoulder.  

Her pupils dilate when she catches their shared reflection. 

His voice turns deep, gruff. “All the better to save you with.” 

Sophie’s fingers cling to his shirt and dig into his skin. Before she can answer, Andrew notices movement on the edge of his vision. It’s a reflex, the way his arm flashes out to catch the falling child. 

This pint-sized human would have tumbled straight into the concrete, bare knees and ice cream be damned, if Andrew hadn’t been right there, thank God — Sophie recounts her husband’s prowess to anyone who will listen. A savior. 

Later, when Andrew overhears the birthday girl’s father discussing the pizza pickup, he offers to assist. He carries nine pies from a trunk to a folding table. His arms ripple. The other guests gasp, and their hands itch to applaud. 

During presents, Andrew watches a young guest — someone’s preteen brother — attempt to snatch a newly-opened toy from the pile. He’s there like lightning, his hand coming between the boy and the remote-control convertible. The boy’s father thanks Andrew for stepping in with his wayward son.  

Andrew’s body is invigorated. His focus is sharp. His only mission left? Bath and bed for the kids before 8pm. Because Sophie needs him.  

He carries her to the car, crossing-the-threshold style, while the kids trail behind shrieking and whooping. She’s giggling, too, burying her face in his straining chest.  

At home, mission accomplished, Andrew pins his wife against the wall with his hips. She runs her hands down his sides. 

“With great power comes great responsibility,” he rumbles against her neck, before he makes love to her with gravity-defying feats of strength and stamina.   

When he finally takes his own shower and sees his clean, smooth face through the fog, he senses an absence. He sighs, and his veins and straining muscles deflate with the exhale.

Another party for his daughter’s circle, and, since this is a real sophisticated soiree, there are two face painters. Andrew won’t have to wait long for a turn, so he lets his son go first. 

He chooses a pirate this time, wondering what a little rebellion will feel like on his skin. 

He keeps his mischief in check throughout the party, only stealing two extra cupcakes to bring home. He knows he’ll be hungry after he plunders Sophie’s treasure. She might be, too, actually. He swipes a third. 

The other parents give his dark swagger a wide berth out of respect. But not his wife. She’s holding a sweating soda and eyeing Andrew from across the lawn, her straw always just out of reach of her searching lips because she can’t bother to tear her eyes away from him to find it.  

He notices a few of the other dads have colorful cheeks and foreheads, too — scorpions, dinosaurs, and panthers, the paint overwhelming their features — while their wives titter with Sophie. She must have let them in on their secret, and the other couples were brave enough to try it.

When the party ends, Sophie scurries to him, and he hoists her over his shoulder. It’s only a few blocks’ walk home, so he carries her the whole way. The kids have run ahead of them this time, chanting a sea shanty they made up that’s also suspiciously reminiscent of a famous theme park ride.  

Row, row, the sea is calling;

We want treasure! We row till morning; 

Yo-ho, yo-ho, we’re a pirate family!

Dinner is a feast of cured meat, cheese, crusty bread, and chicken nuggets, drowned with ale and sparkling water from goblets dug out of the hutch. The kids continue with their shanties through bathtime. Sophie swishes her skirts and beckons Andrew to the bedroom with a crooked finger.     

The stolen cupcakes, slightly squished, fuel them. 

When the next weekend is absent of a party, Andrew’s cheeks are itchingly dry. His jawline seems inordinately weak. He almost considers a trip to the local craft store to see if they carry face paint. He does check online. But, alas, they don’t have it, and Amazon will take three days to deliver, and by that point it will almost be another weekend and another party, and . . .

He doesn’t have to wait long. The preschool is hosting a family carnival, and one of the teachers is filling the role of artist. After watching a few paint jobs, though, Andrew volunteers to do his own.  

He browses the sample photos, though he’s already certain what he’s in the mood for. The jungle-themed party all but cements his decision, with images of the equator's variegated fauna and wildlife inspiring him. Yet, it’s a different variegation that ends up catchin his curiosity — that of a tabby cat. Really, a kitten. He could be so playful; his tongue so rough; his footfalls soft. What if . . .

He glances toward his wife. Sophie is watching him, licking her lips.  

So, instead, he becomes power and potent energy. 

In his tiger form, he stalks through the party, lithe and smooth, sensing and scenting the crowd. His teeth are long, and his claws are sharpened to points. He looks for threats, and, finding none, takes to basking in the courtyard’s sun. The fathers watch him, even attempt to mimic his electric nonchalance in their get-ups. Andrew broadens his shoulders, giving them a good view. 

This time when Sophie joins him, she, too, is painted. He quirks his head, taking in her pink and gold tiara, the swirls across her temples. His heart races. His eyebrows twitch. In all his coolness, he sidles up to her. She is his princess. He, her fierce protector. 

The crowd around them almost cheers, though the other women are more concerned with rushing to join the line for their own flowery paint — now that it’s clearly de rigueur.

When Andrew and Sophie meet in carnal pleasure later that night, he consumes her. Devours her in all her softness. She lets him feast. 

After, when he uses a damp cloth to wipe the paint from her body and his own, an odd sense of insatiate hunger gurgles beneath the relief of shrinking limbs.         

Following the positive reception, Sophie has the enthusiastic idea to learn from YouTube videos, so they can spend their weeknights, too, donned in colors. Andrew, a bear; Sophie, a flower. He, a lion; she, a mouse. A beast and a damsel. Or a tentacled sea monster, with extra dexterity to take out the trash and grab her ass in one pass. It’s intoxicating — motivating — the way she bows under his touch or a glance. 

The kids ignore them, as long as they’re fed and bathed and have clean clothes. He assumes they’re getting their homework done. If he’s not working or checking his email for birthday e-vites, he’s thinking of animals and reminding himself of the way Sophie’s doe eyes darken when she sees his manliness take shape.    

Their colors change with the seasons, and Sophie decides that, this year, they will host a New Year’s block party. They develop a plan — just the right idea, they assure each other giddily: invite their neighbors and friends from their children’s schools, and hire a top artist to travel all the way from The City. They will be celebrated for their ingenuity! 

While the town’s brood of youngsters dance in a cacophony of sparklers and bang snaps, men and women snake around their court, waiting for a turn in the artist’s chair. They huddle against each other to ward against the cold and conspire on their designs. A few of the men even shout barbs down the line – taunts to each other about who will be fiercest or the most virile. The wives demure behind shy eyes and hummed laughs.

Andrew smirks. He, who has bestowed this gift to his neighbors, who has allowed them this chance to enter the new year in a new form, is confident in his choice. Though a rainbow of fireworks caught his attention initially, the menacing flames that now encircle his eyes will light up the night brighter than any glittery spectacle.  

He searches for Sophie to show her. And to feed his fire with her oxygen. He sees her down the block, her back to him. In an instant, he’s there, spinning her toward him, not hiding his plans to engulf her.  

Instead, when he sees what she’s done, the conflagration travels down his whole chest. Its embers sit low in his belly, in his flesh even absent of paint. 

Silver threads fan out across her brow, ladder down her nose, kiss her lips, trace the lines of her jaw and neck. From one temple, a dense, black body lays in wait, its articulated legs — all eight — stretch across her forehead and cheek. One gets lost in the crease of her eyelid. 

“Sophie,” he exhales. He almost tastes the bittersweetness of bait.   

“I thought the colors would match . . . for later,” she says, and he knows. The black nightgown with silver threads that she saves for special occasions — the one she wore for his birthday last year.

Andrew studies her. He traces a finger across each filament. “Black widows eat their mates.”   

Sophie’s hand flies to her mouth, but she can’t hide her blush. 

He draws her fingers away and leans down to her ear. “I’m not scared.” 

Their neighbors’ deferential hush at seeing this peculiar match-up speaks volumes.

When the ball has dropped, when the neighbors have left, when all the hot chocolate has been drunk, and the artist tipped handsomely, Sophie lures Andrew to her web.         

Seeking more, more, more, they push the boundaries of what they thought they knew. Every evening, when Andrew steps through the door from work, he takes stock of his thrumming heart. He settles the children in front of the TV. Then, he and Sophie slough their daywear to reveal a matched fierceness: a shark churning in stormy waves, or wolves stalking each other. She’s a python undulating through their shared space. He’s a piranha, quick and sharp. These new beings keep them up till the earliest hours. And when his alarm blares at 6am each morning, the tedium of attiring himself in the shell of a middle-aged financial analyst makes Andrew’s skin crawl. 

At a birthday party in the spring (who cares who’s), Andrew enters through the flap of a white tent. He absorbs the portraits of great heroes and cartoon royalty, of renowned desert animals and the ocean’s most majestic creatures. Forest nymphs model in gilt frames. As has become custom now at these get-togethers, inspirations line the plastic walls — palaces erected solely for artists to exact transformations. Andrew’s lungs welcome the invasion of clay and chemical chalk. He breathes it into his metamorphosis.           

The artist guides him to a silver chair in the corner. It’s just the two of them inside the opaque, flapping structure. He knows Sophie is next door making her choice. They had let all the other party-goers mutate first, as they prefer to emerge, alchemized, to a captive audience no longer impatient for a turn. 

As he sits, his eye catches a luna moth, painted to extravagance, near one of the tent’s folds. It’s almost dragon-like in its coloration and shape. The subtlety of it nudges at him. The silkiness of the wings. The roundness of its edges. 

Andrew announces his selection and feels only serene anticipation as the striations of experimentation harden and settle across the bridge of his nose. 

When he and Sophie finally exit their respective tents to the anticipating crowd, the gasps drown out the sound of wayward children splashing in the far-off pool. 

Andrew blinks, dips his head. He feels their collective gaze searching for scales or some other pointy thing to excuse his choice.   

Sophie — a battle-hardened warrior — steps forward, waving to their onlookers with a commanding sweep of her arm. Their eyes move to her, the mosaic of their irises mirroring the path of her hand. Away from him. The crowd parts for her, and Andrew looks on as they slowly reform in a loose circle, blocking his view while giving her space to march to the snack table. They follow, salivating.  

As the party continues in its usual beats — games, pizza, presents — Andrew studies: Sophie’s painted disciples shower her with compliments and take turns resting their hands on her arms as if they could melt into her and become one shared, mighty body. 

Andrew tells himself to ignore the whispers of those who relegated him to the edge, where his wings aren’t so pronounced and can better blend with the fence line. He wipes his sweaty palms on his pant legs. They celebrated his change before, he wants to shout to anyone who will listen. 

But they’re too busy turning toward Sophie like she’s their sun.

32 pieces, 32 writers, one theme: what it costs to be seen, and what it costs not to be.

We are watched and don’t know it. We wait to be recognized and are not. When we are noticed, we learn it carries a cost of its own.

The 32 writers range from first publication to fifty years of it, and each arrived at this question on their own.

We didn’t build the issue around it. The issue told us what it was, and we recognized it.

Welcome to the inaugural edition of Inkhorn Review, September 2026.

html:
Harsh metals fall from the sky.
We shelter in the oyster bar
and leave metallurgy to others.

We agree that our planet
must have run over a small
but elemental lump of debris.

The oysters are good this month.
Their life spans may be modest,
but their vacant shells honor

the creature that created them
thanks to twists of evolution
no one could have seen coming.

Some of the falling metal 
has already oxidized greenish
or reddish or black. When

this peculiar storm ends, people
will scoop up the shards to sell
to tourists and eager scientists.

We’ll remain seated and sipping
Tanqueray gin and tonic.
We’ve already eaten a dozen

mildly protesting oysters.
Their shells pile up on a plate
much as the alien sky-elements

collect in the street, sharp edges
daring us to touch them and risk 
wounds too celestial to heal.

html:
I suppose no one would accuse me of indifference. He was a stray dog. People passed through the nearby residential blocks every day; I was not the only one who saw him. None of them stopped to help him. At least I fed him.

After I first saw him, I began to bring him food every day. That afternoon, I had just finished grocery shopping at Aeon and was riding my electric scooter home when I saw him on a small path near my neighborhood. He was a black dog. I don’t know why I stopped. Maybe it was the wounds covering his body. Big and small, some still wet with blood, some already scabbed over. Probably bites from other dogs. Or his eyes. His tail tucked, something in his gaze I couldn’t name. Looking at him, I was reminded of the dogs I had seen as a child outside a dog meat shop, in cages by the entrance. They had that same look in their eyes. My chest tightened. Or maybe he reminded me of the dog I had when I was ten. When we moved to the town, my parents gave her to our neighbors. When I left, she tried to follow me, but the chain around her neck held her back. She stood there, looking at me, whimpering. I walked away. She was still looking at me. I still think of her sometimes. That chain, less than a meter long. She never ran across the grass again. Never lay on her back at my feet, waiting for me to rub her belly. Her world became that small yard. She walked slowly inside it, like an old person with a cane, each step careful, one after another.

For eight days in a row, every evening, I brought a bag of dog food, a bottle of water, and two bowls to that path. At first he hid in the grass, watching me from a distance. I poured the food into one bowl and water into the other. Then I crossed to the other side of the path and stood under a tree, far from him. I smiled at him. He looked at me, then at the bowls. People say animals can sense kindness. I walked away slowly. When I turned back, he was already devouring the food. It was late October. The mornings and evenings were cold. I should have prepared a cardboard box for him, or at least left him some old clothes.

You don’t see many stray dogs in Guangzhou. They say it’s because the public security bureau organizes teams to patrol the streets and capture and relocate them. The nearest holding facility was less than an hour’s drive from my home. I could have called the police, asked them to take him in. Maybe that would have eased my conscience.

But it was already too late. I told myself someone must have taken him away. That he had been hurt.

I shouldn’t have hesitated. I kept wondering whether I should take him home. On the third day, he dared to come closer to me. On the fourth, he wagged his tail and let me touch his head. Even after everything the world had done to him, he still trusted people. He would have been a gentle, obedient dog. He would have known how to cherish a home. If I had taken him in, he would have been my most loyal companion. I wouldn’t have had to come back every day to an empty apartment. He would have been there when I returned from work, sat with me while I ate, walked with me in the evenings, slept beside me at night. We could have been happy together.

I should have decided sooner. If I had acted at once, if I hadn’t let him down, he would be here now, tongue out, grinning at me. But he disappeared. Next to the bowls, there was only a darkened patch of blood. I heard the security guards had driven him away with sticks. I heard someone had complained. I heard they were afraid he might have rabies. He waited on that path every day for me to come back. He knew I would. He thought I cared about him. 

He thought we would become a family.

html:
At the grocery store my son asks
why the lobsters’ claws are taped shut.

So they don’t hurt each other, I say.

He considers this from the cart.

Then why are they together?

The man behind the seafood counter
looks up from wrapping haddock.

Nobody answers.

One lobster climbs over another,
gets halfway up the glass,
slides backward.

My son wants to know
which one we’re taking home.

None of them.

He asks why they’re here.

For people to buy.

Why?

To eat.

He looks at the tank.

The seafood man turns on the faucet
and rinses his knife.

At checkout my son asks
if the lobsters know.

Know what?

That somebody gets to pick.

I put the milk on the belt.
Then the eggs.
Then the chicken.

He reaches from the cart
and turns the chicken
label-side down.
