Alan Katz: I don't have the ability to sing, whereas my son David, as I mentioned, is a musical theater performer. He spent a year playing Peter in the off-Broadway musical Pinkalicious. and he is a wildly talented producer, director, and performer. So we all do things differently. So many people will walk up to me and say, give me a joke, you got a joke? And my friends, I'm sure you're familiar with Dan Gutman, children's author Dan Gutman from the My Weird School series, and Peter Larranges, who is just an incredible writer. He's got books. He just did a babysitter's club book. He's done the 39 clues. He's got a series called Throwback. We have an ongoing text chain where we make each other laugh. And I just love that because humor is finding a way to take something that I see in one way that you might see in a different way. And we build on each other's laughter. And I just love that.

Terry Heath: When your kids were growing up, did they think you were funny?

Alan Katz: I hope so. They are all funny in their own way. My son Nathan, who works in Chicago for Capital One, is not in a creative field, but he's hilarious. I said to him recently, because he does resemble what my father looked like tremendously, very similar. And I just said to him, we were sitting on the couch and I said, you look like my father. And he turned to me in an instant and said, you look like my father, which is just

Terry Heath: Ha ha ha.

Alan Katz: a great, a great line. we all laugh. all, you know, I mentioned Nathan, I mentioned David, I mentioned Simone, my oldest son, Andrew is a speech writer. He worked in politics for a long time. He is very gifted in turning phrases that I could never write. He gets that from Rose and he's also quite funny. So we had a left field household, I'm pretty sure.

Terry Heath: when you're going through your day, do you do you take a notebook and jot down things that you think would be funny somewhere, or do you just keep in your head?

Alan Katz: You know, I always tell kids I keep a notebook handy and I do. have a notebook. Sometimes I'll just dictate it right into the phone. But I will. I do. Writers observe. That's what we do. You know, so many people said to me, my play got your nose here my whole life. But it was hearing Andrew say got your nose and me saying, don't take my nose to Washington, D.C. that led to the book. So maybe writers listen with a different, I don't know, I'm not that smart to know why, but somebody will say something to me and I'll say, that's a good idea for a book. And not everything I write becomes a book. Not everything I write is successful, but it's a joy to be able to take a blank piece of paper or a blank computer screen and turn it into something that only I can write. Even if we're both gonna write about a squirrel. your squirrel is gonna have different abilities and different sensibilities than mine does.

Terry Heath: What would be the hallmark of what you do write? Is there a style you can pin down?

Alan Katz: Well, I think I would say all of my books, the book with Rose will be my 53rd book. I did a couple of books. These are my only, this is one of my only two books that is not fiction silliness. It's called Awesome Achievers in Science and there's also Awesome Achievers in Technology. There are real life profiles of people who have invented things that kids use every day. like the remote control, like Siri on the iPhone, like windshield wipers, Velcro. And I tell you the actual story of the gentleman who invented Velcro. And then there's some humor that not to make fun of their their inventions, but to have fun with how their inventions improve my life. The person who invented the microwave oven, look at all the time he saved me. Look at all the things I can do with that time. So I tell you the story and then. I have some fun with it. By the way, I want to make that distinction. I tell kids and it's certainly there's an essay in each of my joke books that say it's really good to make people laugh, but it's never okay to make a joke at anybody else's expense. I don't care if it's the funniest joke ever. Don't tell a joke that's going to hurt anybody's feelings. If a thousand people are laughing, but one person feels bad because you made fun of their backpack with their jacket or the way they throw a ball, not going to hear it from me. not gonna see it from me. And I think kids are getting that, kindness comes first.

Terry Heath: what was your life like when you were a kid? Were you a funny kid at school or a shy kid or

Alan Katz: I was a funny kid and it was interesting. I was funny, but I wasn't unpopular. Jerry and I did shows every day after lunch, extemporaneous silly shows. But kids used to bully me and say, give me a joke or I'm going to hitch it. And it made no sense that that would be the currency, that a joke would be the currency to stop the bullying. And in fact, my father, who had children's shoe stores, started selling Puma Clyde sneakers at cost to the bullies if they'd leave me alone. And I only realized a few years ago that what that was doing was giving them better footwear with which to chase me.

Terry Heath: Yeah.

Alan Katz: But I wasn't popular, I wasn't unpopular, I was just one of the kids. you know, whereas some would say I'm going to be an athlete, I'm going to be a scientist, I'm going to be a doctor, and indeed, many of them grew up to be that. I knew I wanted to make humor my career. I really did. I wrote for the comedian, Henny Youngman, who you may or may not be aware of, but I wrote

Terry Heath: Yeah.

Alan Katz: jokes for him when I was in high school. $7 a joke. I would send him 20 jokes. He would circle three of them and send me a check for $21. I actually have an incredible picture of the two of us when I was in high school. I can send you. And my parents would say, how do you know he's not using all 20 jokes? And I'd say, he's not going to rip me off. But creating humor is something I've done my whole life.

Terry Heath: And the bullies who threatened to hit you if you didn't come up with a joke taught you how to write for a deadline.

Alan Katz: That's really true. See, the Rosie O'Donnell show was an incredible, incredible deadline filled assignment. And when I got there, there had been 15 writers for five spots on the show and every 13 weeks they would leave because they couldn't write under pressure. Many of them were wonderful standup comics who just didn't know what it was like to sit at a computer at seven in the morning. or eight in the morning and turnout material that had to be live on network TV or national TV at 10 a.m. When I got there, soon after, two of us did the whole show the rest of the way. Rosie was kind enough to realize that the two of us, another writer by the name of Casey St. Ange, she and I did the bulk of the work for the bulk of the five years. And it was pressure, but it was the kind of fun pressure And you know, when you write a book, I mean, the book that Rose and I did, my wife Rose and I did, we wrote it last year. It's coming out next year. That's a two year wait. When you write a Saturday morning cartoon or I've written for the Pinkalicious cartoon series, two years to make a cartoon. When you write for a live television show like the Rosie O'Donnell show, or I later worked for the Tony Danza show, daytime talk show, you write at 8 a.m. it's live and being laughed at and being covered in the news two hours later. What better feedback is there than that?

Terry Heath: Looking back at you as a child, is there anything you would not want to tell yourself as a child that you've learned now?

Alan Katz: That's an interesting question. No, think I had a, I'm going to do this attitude. I mean, I'd say to my parents, I'm going to write. I'm going to be a writer and writers get paid and writers have families and writer. And they, they kind of say, you'll end up in the shoe business or you'll end up being a teacher. There is nothing wrong with the shoe business. is nothing, certainly nothing wrong with being a teacher. But I knew I had the confidence as a 8, 10, 12 year old. I mean, I won writing awards in high school and was writing for Henny Youngman and other comics when I was 17, 18, 19 years old. I knew I carved out a path and looking back now, that's a long time ago, looking back, there are jobs I wouldn't have taken or jobs I would have taken that I didn't. But what a joy to be able to make people laugh and that's how I pay my bills.

Terry Heath: Was there anybody who believed in you when you were a child? You said you believed in yourself, but was there anyone else?

Alan Katz: Yes, my high school English teacher, Mildred Feinsilver, I have dedicated some books to her, several books to her. She's the one who said, take it seriously and you'll do it. Now, it's funny to say, take being a comedy writer seriously, but that's what I had to do. You know, there were shows that I tried to get, Rose and I moved to LA for three years in the 90s and desperately tried to get on a sitcom, couldn't do it. My sample scripts weren't good enough or I wasn't tall enough or I don't know what the reason was. It hasn't been a straight trajectory, you know, to, to fame and or fortune, but I zig and I zag, you know, it's interesting. I had an agent when I was in LA and he said, only write for television. Don't do animation, which is television, but only write for sitcoms is what he meant. Don't do books. Don't do animation. don't do game shows, don't write for corporate America. And I said, no, no, that's what I want to do because when I don't have a job in television, hey, there are books. When my books aren't as popular, I take an animation job or a sales promotion job, you know, and it's all good. Writers can do many different things.

Terry Heath: You're self employed, are you a good boss?

Alan Katz: Well, I'm... I'm not the biggest self proponent of getting it done right now. I have never learned that if it's due next Monday, I could finish it today and be done. I will finish it Sunday. And I think some of it is creating pressure that leads to better work because certainly I can work under pressure. proved that on the Rosie O'Donnell show and the Tony Danza show and some other shows, but There are people who just get it done. And I'm sort of never been that way, but that's okay. I don't miss deadlines, but I make them by the skin of my teeth.

Terry Heath: Is there anybody whose career you tried to emulate or maybe somebody that you're jealous of that you would secretly like their career?

Alan Katz: No, listen, you I was a very, very, very big Suppy Sales fan. He was a childhood comedic god to me. And late in my career, or late in his life, I should say, I got to meet him and work with him a little bit. I actually booked him on the Rosie O'Donnell Show as a guest when he had a book come out. But, you know, I don't think jealous is the right word. I so admire people who do what I do. and do it well. Other authors I mentioned, Dan Gutman, he's a superstar. He really is. I just admire people who do what they do well.

Terry Heath: Tell me a story about when luck really moved you forward in your career.

Alan Katz: I think my whole career is luck. It's just, you know, it's funny. My son David is a freelancer and I tell him my advice as a freelancer because he's the only one of my kids who's relying on the phone to ring. And I always say, say yes to everything you can do and do well. I have turned down work because I wouldn't be the right person for it or I wouldn't have enough time to do it. But he's 26 and when somebody says, could you perform this or could you produce this? I say, you never know what room you're going to be in that's going to lead to your next room and your next thing. So I think it's a luck of being good enough to do a good job when I'm smart enough to say yes.

Terry Heath: What's the most unglamorous thing that you've done this week? People think of writers and and celebrities as having these glamorous lives and we know it's work, but what's the what's the most down in the ditches thing you've had to do?

Alan Katz: See, I don't, I mean, it's called life. I mean, if I tell you I got an oil change, does that make me anything different than

Terry Heath: Ha ha.

Alan Katz: everybody else who drives a car? I'm not particularly handy. I don't mow my own lawn. I don't know how to. I'm fortunate enough that I have a, Very supportive family. show my kids and my wife everything I write. And they're very perceptive in what stays and what goes. They're not always right, but neither am I. I don't have, nope, I don't have a glamorous life. I'm not famous. You know, one of the things I do when I visit a school and they all want my autograph, I want their autographs. I say, your writers too. I'm not the only writer. If I were an astronaut, And I've been on a lunar mission. I'd be the only one in this building who has completed a lunar mission. That's not the case. I use the same letters of the alphabet that you do. We're all writers. And if you're not writing every day, what are you wasting your time? You you should be doing that. This piece of paper could either be my next book or it could be my shopping list. But either way, it's going to involve thinking. It's going to involve writing. That makes me sound much smarter than I am, by the way.

Terry Heath: Yeah. What would you tell somebody who wants to get into comedy writing?

Alan Katz: I'd say we don't need them. We have enough.

Terry Heath: Ha ha

Alan Katz: I don't need the competition. No, mean, listen, comedy writing has changed over the years. When I started, you wrote something, someone performed it, someone produced it, someone printed it. These days, anybody with an iPhone can make a movie or a podcast or print a book. know, stay away from AI. Use your own creativity, I beg you. But everybody who wants a shot can take their best shot these days. And I would encourage everybody, you think you're funny, get out there and be a standup or write a funny book or make a funny movie. We can do it.

Terry Heath: What do you think of writers today?

Alan Katz: I meet so many writers. visit a lot of schools, as I mentioned. There are other writers there. I speak at conventions, book festivals. There's a book festival coming up in late September. The Chappaqua Children's Book Festival in Chappaqua, New York. 150 authors and illustrators. And by the way, a salute to all the illustrators who have brought my books to life. Because very few of my books are just words. They all have pictures. Writers are doing some incredible things. You know, I see books and nobody's jealous of each other. I root for my friend's success and for other people's success. If somebody says to me, I wish I thought of that, that's a compliment. We're not competing. There's enough paper out there for each to print a book.

Terry Heath: It it seems like there aren't a lot of sitcoms being written anymore. What what happened?

Alan Katz: It really aren't.

Terry Heath: What happened to the sitcom?

Alan Katz: Well, I suppose what happened is the internet and YouTube and attention spans. I look at all the daytime talk shows there were back with Rosie and Ellen and Tony Danza and Howie Mandel had one. And so many people had daytime talk shows. Kelly Clarkson just went off. Jennifer Hudson is going away. I guess it's just simpler to pick up the phone and Look at who you want to. Rosie said something the other day in an interview. She said if she ever did a show again, I'm paraphrasing, but if she ever did a show again, it wouldn't be a celebrity show because if Tom Hanks wants to promote his movie, he can do it online. He can do it in so many ways that wasn't possible back when we did five shows a week, 195 shows a year for five years. She did it for six years. I was there for five. So things have changed. I sitcoms are wildly expensive and reality programming is much cheaper and you don't have to invest. mean, Friends wouldn't happen now. Everybody loves Raymond, probably couldn't happen now. The markets are changing. know, Kimmel is hanging on by a thread. Jimmy Fallon's hanging on by a thread. Colbert was sent away. Entertainment has changed so much.

Terry Heath: Do you have a picture of where you think it's going to be in five years or maybe ten years?

Alan Katz: Boy, I sure don't know him, but I can't wait to find out.

Terry Heath: Yeah.

Alan Katz: You know, as I said, I did some books that it was a very small publisher and they did an awesome job with them. You've seen the books like Who Was, where it's like who was Mozart or who was John Kennedy. Taking a humorous look at it, I said, who wasn't that person? And I did lyographies, the lyography. of Thomas Edison, the absolutely untrue, totally made up, 100 % fake life story of the world's greatest inventor. There's one about Babe Ruth. There's one about Amelia Earhart. Not a shred of truth in the whole book. Hopefully kids laugh their heads off at my exploits. And then the last chapter says, okay, now that you know the biography of Thomas Edison, here's his real story, go find out more. All I'm trying to do is get the kids to enjoy reading. laugh their heads off, then they put their heads back on and learn the real story. I visited schools where kids say, can we write a biography together? And I say, sure, now these are kids who weren't thinking about writing, weren't interested in writing. We will sit down and they'll say, here's the biography of George Washington. know, George Washington was born at 8.02 AM in Memorial Hospital and he became president later that day. Whatever they write

Terry Heath: Yeah.

Alan Katz: is pure nonsense, pure imagination. I'm not saying be wrong all the time. I'm not saying skip the facts. Teachers are using these as a way to do compare and contrast. Mr. Katz said this, here's the real story. So they're laughing, they're learning, they're seeing the difference between creativity and nonsense. I mean, there's a famous meme that says, don't believe everything you read on the internet. and it's attributed to Abraham Lincoln.

Terry Heath: Mm-hmm.

Alan Katz: Just silliness. So if I can help kids find their silly bone, their funny bone, and help them say, wait a minute, I can be creative too, that's a good lesson for everybody. so what I started to say, I'm sorry, is I've thought about doing these as podcasts. Where one chapter a week kids can listen to them. There are podcasts out there like a young Benjamin Franklin. And they're like old time radio dramas. There's a person, an older voice saying, you know, I wasn't always an elder statesman. Fact is, when I was a kid, I sold newspapers on the street and you hear transitional music and you hear kids saying, get your paper, get your paper. Mr. Want to buy a paper? And it's a news story about Benjamin Franklin. I could do lyographies as weekly chapters that kids could listen to. Other ways of taking content and putting it out there in a different form.

Terry Heath: you said earlier the there's a story behind your name that you would tell me later. What's that story?

Alan Katz: Yes, I have two stories about my name. One is that on World Read-Aloud Day, which is a day in early February, where many authors and illustrators and creators visit schools virtually on a Zoom or Google Meet. And it's a volunteer thing just to spark the love of books and reading. And every year I get two or three requests when the window to invite me is open and they invite me and then I say yes. And then they write to the whole school saying, I got him. got Alan Gratz. Now Alan Gratz with a GR instead of a K is an incredible author of middle grade fiction. I am not Alan Gratz. I write, me out of the bathtub and Got your nose. And I write back to these people and say, just to be clear, I'm Alan Katz, not Alan Gratz. And they write back, I don't know who you are. Thanks

Terry Heath: Yeah.

Alan Katz: anyway. So I'm confused for Alan Gratz quite often. There are times where if you go to an online bookseller, which I don't recommend you do, you should always buy at your local independent bookstore, but keep them going. But... If you Google my name, you will come up with Alan Gratz very often in terms of online booksellers. There's also another television writer by the name of Alan Katz. Not me. He has two L's. I have one. And a few years ago, he was mailed the royalties that were meant for me to, for residuals, I should say, for my television writing, he got the check. And he wrote to me and said, I'm sorry, let me return the check. It was a common mistake and easy mistake to make. And then he told me, actually, my name isn't Alan Katz anymore. And I said, what do you mean? Turns out he made a movie called Big Man on Campus. It was kind of an Animal House type movie. And he starred in it. And it was his dream in life to bring his parents to the movie theater and have it say Big Man on Campus. And the next slide would say starring Alan Katz. And he called the screen actors, Geldens, okay, I made a movie. I would like to register my name as Alan Katz. And they said, you can't, there's already an Alan Katz who's a performer, not me, but another Alan Katz. They said, you can be Alan Michael Katz. You can be Michael Katz. You can be Alan Katz. You can be A.M. Katz, but you can't be Alan Katz. And he said, but I wanted to say starring Alan Katz. And they said, you can't. He legally changed his name. and I saw his social security card. He legally changed his name from Alan Katz, which could not appear in the movie, to starring Alan Katz. So on the movie, when it says big man on campus, and then it says starring Alan Katz, that is his name, as opposed to it saying starring Meryl Streep or starring Tom Cruise, it says starring Alan Katz and that's his legal name now. So those are my two Alan Katz stories. I'm not Alan Gratz. I'm not starring Alan Katz. I'm simply Alan Katz. And you'll find them, that name on many of my books.

Terry Heath: Okay, then what's next for Alan Katz?

Alan Katz: Well, next is the book with Rose. Well, the joke book I mentioned and the book with Rose. We're doing a musical of the Silly Dilly Musical. We'll be at the Westport Playhouse here in Connecticut coming up in a few weeks. Working on some new game show ideas. I've worked a lot in game shows. you know what? What's next is I don't know. It's a... A whole lot of things on my desk that could turn into my next book, my next TV show, a podcast. And again, that's what I love about writing. I actually, I'll show you one more thing. I worked for a trading card company in the nineties and we did 660 Elvis Presley cards. We did 220 Beatles cards and I invented these. They're called Barbie Fashion Play cards. So there's a beautiful picture of Barbie. You flip it open, she has a new hairdo. Flip it another way, she has a new skirt. There are 27 different ways to mix and match the fashions. On the back is a story about Barbie. Flip it over, it has a new ending and a new beginning. And they all still make sense, 27 different stories to tell. I visit schools, kids make their own fashion play cards. So it's spreading the creativity. That's what my goal is. If you ask me, you kind of did ask, what do I see in 10 years? More of what I do? more school visits, more ways to unearth and unlock the creative powers within young readers and writers everywhere.

Terry Heath: You knew you wanted to write comedy when you were a kid. It did it turn out the way that you thought it would? Is it does does what you live today look like what you thought it would look like as a kid?

Alan Katz: Yeah, I think so. listen, I've done hundreds of projects that you've never seen, you've never heard about, you never knew I wrote. But that's what puts the food on the table sometimes, know, writing, sales meeting game shows, sales training game shows about pharmaceuticals. That's not something that I would have aspired to. But when somebody says, can you do this? And I can do it well, and I become an expert. I've written funny films about ingredients that go into gluten-free foods, things like that. It's like, wait a minute. You need humor. You need clarity. You need attention to detail. I check all those boxes. That's OK. Has Mel Brooks ever written a gluten-free film? No. Did I want to be Mel Brooks? Maybe. But there is one of those. We already have a Mel Brooks. So I aspire to just keep doing what I do and keep doing it better, to not find new ways to make people laugh, and to encourage, as I said, to encourage young readers and writers.

Terry Heath: Has it been worth it?

Alan Katz: Well, sure, absolutely. Yeah, I mean, I'm proud of everything I've done and proud of the sensibilities that I've been able to share and pass on to our children and proud of them, proud of my wife. Yeah, of course, it's been worth it. Has anybody ever told you it wasn't worth it? They wish they hadn't done it.

Terry Heath: No, no, not yet.

Alan Katz: I mean, I did stand up twice and do I wish I had done more of that? Maybe. Do I wish I had done more radio? I'm on the radio quite a bit being interviewed about books and different projects. Do I wish I'd done more public speaking? Sure. You know, I've done keynote speeches at Literacy conferences, as I mentioned, I visit a ton of schools every year. So I'm kind of a standup comic in the sense, but I'm a standup comic with books to talk about and a love of reading and writing. So often the last few years since COVID, I'll visit a school and I'll say to kids, as the groups are coming in, I'll engage the kids in the front and I'll say, what are you reading these days? And kids are saying, I'm not reading. It's like, well, you must be reading something. It's like, I read what I have to for school. It's like, what about pleasure reading? kids, not all of them, of course, but a lot of them are saying, I don't read for pleasure. It's like, that doesn't make any sense. We got to get kids reading more. We got to get kids writing more. You know, I tell kids, you know, so many people here, I showed you these got your nose. Kids will say to me here, I wrote this. It's not very good. I don't want to hear it's not very good. You created it. You succeeded in turning a piece of paper into something that shows your ideas, your illustrations, your creativity. You know, here, after having a good checkup, the year goes to the earring store to get a present for itself. The year chooses a purple hard earring with gold trim. That's somebody's creativity. Now, the fact that I inspired it with my book, Got Your Nose, makes me feel really good. But the fact that they did it should make them feel really good. We're here to inspire each other. I sound like a much nicer person than I really am, but

Terry Heath: Ha ha.

Alan Katz: it's true. One of the things I say in schools is no matter what job you want to be when you grow up, you can achieve that. If you work hard and you put in the reading and writing now, 99 percent of the time a hand will go up and say, I'm to be a football player. I don't even know how to read. What do I need to know how to read for? And I said, fine. When they hand you the playbook and you don't know what it says, how are you going to be a football player? They go, yeah. Kid will say to me, I want to be an astronaut. That doesn't involve writing. I say, well, yes, it does. You have to be a writer to find out what you need to do to be an astronaut and to apply for, you know, you think they let you in, NASA opens the door and says, come on in. No, you've got, you know, so we're all readers. We're all writers. We all use, in fact, there are times I visit a school and I'll say, we all use the same 24 letters of the alphabet. And they go, yeah, that sounds about right. Nobody stops me. And I hate

Terry Heath: Mm.

Alan Katz: that. know, there are kids, teachers are doing such a phenomenal job bringing kids into the reading and writing that they need to do for success and math and science and all that. But it seems like since COVID, kids are not doing the work that they need to. And if they're doing it, they're doing it begrudgingly. And I say, if you haven't read a book, it's not, I'm not the first person to say this, but if you haven't read a book, that you like, you just haven't found the right book yet. And I leave them by saying, keep reading, keep writing, keep laughing, keep singing, most of all, keep being kind to each other. Those are important things. And if we all do those every day, there's success in everybody's future.

Terry Heath: Great. Well well thank you, Alan. cats, not grats. Gratz one L

Alan Katz: cats, right, not grats and Alan with one L and not starring as a future. Thank

Terry Heath: Ha ha ha ha.

Alan Katz: you. Thank you for what you're doing to unearth the wisdom behind reading and writing and all that. I don't suggest that anybody try for my career, but build their own careers. Whether it's writing for pleasure or writing as a career, it's something we can all do and it's something we should all do.

▶ Listen to this episode · 50 min

Alan Katz has written more than 50 books and spent five years writing for The Rosie O'Donnell Show. He grew up in a family of shoe-store owners and teachers and announced early that he'd be a writer — his father's response was that as a writer, you are your own merchandise. We talk about what that life has cost, the bullies who taught him to write on deadline, and why he tells kids a joke at someone else's expense is never worth it.

Topics & Timestamps
  • "You are your own merchandise": the cost of a career where next year is never guaranteed
  • Comedy writing in advertising — Pepsi, McDonald's, and a musical about Sperry computers starring Kirk Douglas
  • Writing song parodies on the 5am train for a show that aired at 10
  • How his daughter's dinner-table question became Take Me Out of the Bathtub
  • Writing jokes for Henny Youngman at $7 apiece, in high school
  • The agent who said write only for television, and why he refused
  • What happened to the sitcom
  • Kids who say they don't read for pleasure

tags.description: Life on Words is an interview show about the writing life as a career: the years, the money, the rejections. Every conversation turns on one question: what has your life in words cost you, and what has it given you back? Guests are novelists, poets, songwriters, agents, editors, publishers, and booksellers. Some have sixty books and major awards. Some have a debut coming out and a day job. Not how they write, but how they've lived it, and the answers are rarely what you'd predict.

▶ Listen to this episode · 1h 2m

Steamy romance novelist Christina Braver has never turned a profit on her books — and she's never regretted a page. In this conversation, Christina talks about writing "real sex representation" into the romance genre: heroines with endometriosis, sexual trauma, and bodies that don't work perfectly, who are still worthy of love and a happy ending. She shares the reader letter she returns to when imposter syndrome hits, the one-star review her Formula One–obsessed son wanted to answer personally, and why a woman with a clinical psychology background and a corporate career ended up writing romance during COVID. Along the way: the "generative stage" of life, the tyranny of the checklist, charlatans in the self-publishing space, and what her husband's coworkers think when they find out what his wife does for a living.

The main question of this podcast: What has your life in books cost you, and what has it given you?

  • (34:34) Where ideas come from: Michael Pollan, Mary Roach's Bonk, and the vet tech who explains boyfriends via animal husbandry
  • (38:17) Writing young men — bro culture, toxic messaging, and the new adult WIP
  • (40:41) Has writing changed her? ("My therapist says my word is why.")
  • (42:18) What she wouldn't tell her younger self — and what she would
  • (47:00) What everyone gets wrong about the job: Nashville dreams and the myth of making it
  • (50:39) The most unglamorous thing she did this week (a tent was involved)
  • (51:28) A day in the writing life: email as the frog, sprint partners, Tuesdays as flex days
  • (55:44) Boundaries, budgets, and refusing the "you should" advice
  • (01:00:05) On a scale of one to ten — was it worth it?

▶ Listen to this episode · 1h 3m

Ben Rockwood and his wife Tamara started Bainbridge Island Press out of frustration — she was writing better and better work and getting nothing but silence from publishers. So they decided to get on the other side of the fence and find out why. Four years later he's designing books, sitting in working groups with Penguin Random House, and helping write an international standard for royalty reporting. He also rejected the show's opening question, which results in an interesting answer.

tags.description: Life on Words is an interview show about the writing life as a career: the years, the money, the rejections. Every conversation turns on one question: what has your life in words cost you, and what has it given you back? Guests are novelists, poets, songwriters, agents, editors, publishers, and booksellers. Some have sixty books and major awards. Some have a debut coming out and a day job. Not how they write, but how they've lived it, and the answers are rarely what you'd predict.

▶ Listen to this episode · 1h 1m

Susan Wiggs sold her first book in 1986 while teaching full-time with a one-year-old at home. She's since written more than 60 novels, won three RITAs, and hit the New York Times, USA Today, and Publishers Weekly bestseller lists. We talk about what that life has cost — a decade of television, some friendships, the steadiness of a predictable paycheck — and what it's given back. Also: the insecurity that never leaves, the bicycle wreck that nearly stopped her, and why she says you have to be ready when your luck comes around.

  • Why she'd rather be called a writer than an author

  • Book signings where nobody came

tags.name: Podcast
tags.description: Life on Words is an interview show about the writing life as a career: the years, the money, the rejections. Every conversation turns on one question: what has your life in words cost you, and what has it given you back? Guests are novelists, poets, songwriters, agents, editors, publishers, and booksellers. Some have sixty books and major awards. Some have a debut coming out and a day job. Not how they write, but how they've lived it, and the answers are rarely what you'd predict.
